Michigan State commit Grayson Thurston still thinking big
articles.content: Grayson Thurston took a large load off his shoulders Saturday evening. The current junior at Warren De La Salle and one of the top junior quarterbacks in Michigan, made a pledge to commit to Michigan State University and play for coach Pat Fitzgerald in 2028. Thurston was a highly sought after QB, collecting interest from a wide variety of NCAA Division I schools, including University of Minnesota, Iowa, Cincinnati, Western Michigan, Bowling Green State, Miami-Ohio and a host of others. He made his pledge Saturday before the Spartans’ game with the University of Washington. “I’m kind of glad I did it now so I don’t have to think about it next season,” said Thurston, a 6-foot-2, 180-pound signal caller who had led De La Salle to back-to-back deep state tournament runs in Division 3, including the state semifinals last year and regional finals this year. “I can really just work (towards) next year and see what we can do. “I am really pumped for next year because we bring back a lot of very good players. We have some nice slot receivers and (running) backs and we still have some good linemen on the team, although we lose some this year. Our goal will be to contend for the state championship.” According to 247 Sports Composite Rankings, Thurston is ranked as the No. 13 player in Michigan, the No. 41-rated quarterback in the nation and top 600 in terms of overall players. Thurston is a two-year starter at quarterback at Warren De La Salle after serving as backup as a freshman. He played some junior varsity and varsity as a 9th grader under the five-quarter rule before taking over the starting role on varsity in 2025. This past season – which ended last Friday night in a 38-13 loss to Harper Woods in a Division 3 regional finals clash – Thurston combined for a combined 17 passing and rushing touchdowns and passed for over 1,200 yards despite playing in only seven of the Pilots’ games. De La Salle’s Game 2 opponent forfeited the night before the contest, while he was hurt but still played in a Week 3 loss to Birmingham Brother Rice (31-28). Thurston came back in Week 9 of the regular season and played in all three postseason games for the Pilots. He played in 22 quarters because of the Week 3 injury plus the Week 2 forfeit win. He also played junior-varsity golf the past two years for De La Salle and will likely play that sport for fun this spring. “I’m not that good to be honest,” joked Thurston, who has grown up in the Shelby Township-Washington Township area. “I just do it for fun.” Thurston grew up in an athletics-minded family. His father Eric Thuston was a four-year starter as a forward in basketball at Rochester High School (1989-1993) while his uncle Bill Thurston was a two-sport standout at Rochester as well (Class of 1990), serving as a standout punter and tight end in football and as a power forward. Both ended up being All-State and played small college athletics. Thurston has already been voted All-CHSL and All-Macomb County Tier 1 teams despite not playing a full season this fall, while should be at least a candidate for various All-Area and All-State honors for various publications. “I am really looking forward to it. But I have some time,” said Thurston, who still has 1.5 years of high school still left before he departs to East Lansing. “Michigan State really liked me and I felt like they really wanted me and they really care about my growth. Their program has a lot of trajectory and I feel the coaches are going to be there a while. Coach Fitzgerald, Coach (Nick) Sheridan are all going to be there for a while. I feel like Michigan State should be pretty good (in the future).”

articles.title: Brad Pitt Explains Why Leonardo DiCaprio’s Cameo in ‘Cliff Booth’ Movie Fell Apart
articles.description: The actor told The Hollywood Reporter at the L.A. premiere that a Rick Dalton appearance in the sequel would have "required a lot of prosthetics."
articles.content: The actor told The Hollywood Reporter at the L.A. premiere that a Rick Dalton appearance in the sequel would have "required a lot of prosthetics." Though Brad Pitt and Leonardo DiCaprio both starred in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, only Pitt appears in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth — and the star is shedding some light on why. Cliff Booth is a follow-up to 2019’s Once Upon a Time, this time centered on Pitt’s stuntman character and set eight years after Quentin Tarantino’s original film. Tarantino wrote the script for the new film with David Fincher taking over as director, and DiCaprio confirmed to Deadline last year that his leading man Rick Dalton is not along for the ride this time, even in a cameo capacity. “There were some talks about it early on. Ultimately, I cannot wait to see the Cliff Booth story, but I’m not in it,” he told the outlet. “I think David Fincher’s the perfect man for the job. Quentin is a huge fan of his work, I’m a huge fan of his work, and there’s nobody better to carry on that lineage and tell that story. I think it’s the next phase of Cliff Booth’s life. I’m excited to see it.” At the Los Angeles premiere on Monday, Pitt told The Hollywood Reporter that a DiCaprio appearance “would have been great fun, but it required a lot of prosthetics, which is a good couple of weeks prepping to get him. It’s hardly worth the cost for a cameo.” There is a joke in the trailer where Booth explains he no longer doubles for DiCaprio’s character because “Rick got too fat,” which is likely where prosthetics would have come into play. “It was talked about for a while, but it just seemed like a big ask,” he added, teasing that they still make a couple of “sweet tributes” to Rick Dalton in the sequel. Both Pitt and DiCaprio earned Oscar nominations for their Once Upon a Time performances, with Pitt going on to win. The follow-up film sees Cliff Booth having left Rick and his stunt career behind, working as a bartender, a projectionist and a Hollywood fixer in the town’s dark underbelly. Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller round out the cast. Also on the carpet, Pitt said he did not expect to reprise the character, but “Quentin was talking about for his 10th one he wanted to do this again — his last film, as he says — and he just wanted to work with friends and do something he loved and I was really flattered. And then he went, ‘Nah!'” Tarantino has previously put together The Movie Critic as his so-called final film, which later evolved into a Once Upon a Time in Hollywood spinoff that he put on the shelf. “I don’t bemoan that all because it’s such a commitment, especially for a director. Two years of their lives,” Pitt continued. “And then things sat around for about nine months and Fincher and I were talking about doing something again and it just happened. It occurred to me, gave it to him, called him, and within 24 hours,” they had the movie in motion. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth starts its IMAX run on Nov. 25 and starts streaming Dec. 23 on Netflix. articles.title: EGLE releases roadmap to rein in climate change contributions from Michigan industry
articles.description: Putting the full plan into action could require a lot of funding at first. But Michigan's chief climate officer says that will make things cheaper for consumers in the long term.
articles.content:
The Great Lakes dominate this true-color Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) image. Lake Superior covers the upper left corner. Beneath it is Lake Michigan, and to the right is Lake Huron. Under Lake Huron is Lake Erie (left) and Lake Ontario (right). The pale blue swirls in Lake Michigan are probably caused by a phytoplankton bloom or calcium carbonate (chalk) from the lake's limestone floor. Concrete-grey patches mark the locations of several cities throughout the Great Lakes region.(Jeff Schmaltz
/ MODIS Rapid Response Team, NASA/GSFC)A new state report has detailed how Michigan’s industrial sector can go carbon-neutral by 2050.The roadmap involves grant programs, tax credits, and capping greenhouse gas emissions while investing in renewable energy and storage. It began as part of the MI Healthy Climate Action plan, released in April 2022.Michigan Chief Climate Officer Alessandra Carreon said it’s not “theoretical.”“It’s grounded in … technology that exists today and practical policy measures, again, that are designed to introduce cost effectiveness for business that translates into cost savings for community members,” Carreon said.The report breaks steps down into three phases: near, medium, and longer-term goals. For the nearer term goals to get done within the next few years, the state needs to start putting resources together, working with stakeholders, and conducting research, the report says.Putting the full plan into action could require a lot of funding and other resources. But Carreon said the more efficient Michigan’s industries can get on the front end, the cheaper things can get down the line.“It can become easy to say this is really expensive and therefore we shouldn’t do it. But if we don’t think about all the externalized costs that result when you sort of stop there, you’re actually incurring costs, again at the system level, that you could be avoiding,” she said.The roadmap estimates industrial emissions could cost the state over $616 million in extra annual health spending by 2050 if nothing changes.Meanwhile, the roadmap authors suggest going all-in on the strategy could lead to lower energy costs. Michigan’s industrial and energy sectors account for nearly half of the state’s greenhouse gas emissions, according to the report.The plan argues coordination between industry and utilities could lead to a more efficient and cheaper energy grid.Elizabeth Boatman is with 5 Lakes Energy, the firm that created the report. She used renewable energy as an example.Boatman said peak hours for renewable energy production don’t always line up with the peak hours for residential use. Without proper storage, some of that excess energy would just get wasted.But, Boatman said, by building more storage capacity and changing power usage habits during those peak renewable production hours, industrial operations could help solve the problem.“The more that we have different ways to offtake electricity when there’s excess of it going into the grid ... the more that we can [level] rates and affordability across all the ratepayers,” Boatman said. “Michigan could serve the same amount of load on the customer side by building less solar and less wind in total.”She said businesses have another reason to stop relying so much on natural gas, as availability and supply chain risks increase.“It’s not hospitals that have their gas shut off because not enough gas can be brought into a state. It’s not homes or universities or police stations. It’s manufacturers,” she said.Other pieces of the plan involve boosting the "Buy Clean, Buy Michigan" plan to encourage more sustainable practices when it comes to sourcing.The Michigan Manufacturers Association said it was still evaluating the plan Monday afternoon and couldn’t weigh in yet. But spokesperson Delaney McKinley said the group believes in working with regulators on future policies.“Our initial review appreciates the report's recognition of the diversity of Michigan's manufacturing industries and the different operational and energy needs across those sectors," McKinley said in an email."As the state looks to support investment in manufacturing, there are opportunities to help manufacturers modernize their operations through voluntary, incentive-based programs such as grants, technical assistance, financing and support for adopting new technologies," said McKinley. "These investments can improve efficiency, strengthen operations, and continue to deliver environmental benefits while keeping Michigan manufacturers competitive.”

articles.title: Family identifies Roseville couple allegedly shot to death by their adult son
articles.content: The husband and wife found shot to death inside of their Roseville this past weekend have been identified by family members while police prepare to file criminal charges against the couple’s adult son. According to a TV news report, the couple’s daughter identified the deceased as Robert and Suzette Giamportone. Their bodies were discovered early Sunday, Nov. 15 after police responded to reports of their 31-year-old son causing a disturbance in the street and noticed shattered glass on the door of their home. The sister of Suzette Giamportone, 62, who did not identify herself, said the family is shocked and heartbroken about the tragic incident. She did not want to speak on camera but said the family is devastated and is asking for privacy as they grieve. The deceased couple’s son has endured mental health issues and was not taking his medication, the sister told WXYZ-TV. She said his parents were trying to get him back on his feet and stabilized. According to the Roseville Police Department, officers responded to the 30000 block of Bluehill Street about 5 a.m. Sunday after receiving reports that the suspect was screaming on their front lawns. While detaining the subject, officers noticed a shattered door at a nearby residence, said Roseville Police Chief Scott Burley. Neighbors told the Macomb Daily they awakened by the suspect had been yelling in what sounded to be a different language for about a half hour before officers responded. The suspect’s ex-girlfriend, with whom he shares a child, told WXYZ that before the deaths, his mother had told her that he had “good days and bad days but was no longer his normal self.” Some of the suspect’s friends said he had been acting manic and paranoid in recent weeks, and had been displaying erratic behavior in the days leading up to the shooting. The suspect is being held at the Macomb County Jail in Mount Clemens while prosecutors consider charges. Roseville man in custody after parents shot to death

Clean sweep as 3 candidates endorsed by Mamdani win primaries in New York
articles.source: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content: All of the mayor's candidates won, ousting two Democratic incumbents. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani flexed his political muscle Tuesday, getting a clean sweep as his three endorsed congressional candidates advanced to November’s general election, ousting two incumbent Democratic congressmen. There were several high-profile races across New York on Tuesday, as well as primaries in Maryland and Utah and primary runoffs in South Carolina. In New York's 7th Congressional District, ABC News projects that Mamdani-backed state Assemblywoman Claire Valdez will win over Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso. In the 10th District, another Mamdani-backed candidate, former city comptroller Brad Lander will beat incumbent Rep. Dan Goldman, ABC News projects. And in the 13th District, the mayor’s candidate, community advocate Darializa Avila Chevalier, will beat incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat, ABC News projects. In an upstate race to replace retiring New York Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik, ABC News projects businessman Anthony Constantino, who made headlines in 2024 for placing a large “Vote for Trump” sign atop his Mohawk Valley Sticker Mule factory, will be the Republican nominee in the 21st District. Constantino was supported by President Donald Trump, who released a video in support of his endorsee on Monday. The race highlighted a divide in the Empire State’s Republican Party, with the chair of the New York Republican State Committee backing Robert Smullen, a state assemblyman and retired Marine Corps officer. Constantino will face dairy farmer Blake Gendebien, who ABC News projects will win the Democratic nomination, in November. And in another race that could determine control of Congress, ABC News projects that former National Security Council Counterterrorism Director Cait Conley will win the Democratic primary to take on Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in the purple 17th District. Maryland state Delegate Adrian Boafo is projected by ABC News to win the Democratic nomination to succeed retiring Rep. Steny Hoyer in the state's 5th District. A former aide to Hoyer, Boafo received the longtime congressman's endorsement, as well as those of Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks in a crowded primary. ABC News projects Moore will win the Democratic primary for governor. Moore is widely seen as a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate. He'll face state Del. Dan Cox, who ABC News projects will win the Republican primary, in a rematch of the 2022 governor's race. South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson will win the runoff in the state's Republican gubernatorial primary, ABC News projects. Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette finished first in the primary after an endorsement by President Donald Trump, but didn't get the necessary 50% of the vote to win outright. Last Friday, Trump announced he was endorsing both Evette and Wilson. Wilson was also endorsed by South Carolina Republican Reps. Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman after they were eliminated in the primary. Wilson will face state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, who won the Democratic primary. Former U.S. Rep. Ben McAdams will win the Democratic primary in Utah’s 1st District, ABC News projects, a district that Democrats hope to flip in the midterms after Utah’s court-ordered redistricting produced the solidly blue district around Salt Lake City. McAdams will face Naval Reserve officer and former Trump White House analyst Riley Owen, who Republicans nominated at their convention in November. 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

articles.title: Paraguay’s ousted president moved to military prison after reports of gym and suite in custody
articles.content: ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay (AP) — A Paraguayan judge on Monday ordered former President Santiago Peña moved out of a suite with a private gym and into a military prison as he awaits trial over the collapse of a major digital bank that toppled his government earlier this month. Judge Osmar Legal ordered Peña transferred from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital, Asunción, where photos published by local media showed that his quarters also included a private bathroom, well-furnished office and spacious dining area. Under the court order, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, Peña will be held at the Viñas Cué military prison, apart from other detainees. He arrived there Monday afternoon, his 48th birthday, in handcuffs, a helmet and a bulletproof vest. President Pedro Alliana opened a news conference Monday by announcing that he had ordered the dismissal of the regiment’s commander, Col. José David Daiub, following allegations that Peña had received special treatment there. Alliana, who served as Peña’s vice president, pledged to give prosecutors whatever resources they need to investigate the bank’s collapse. “Paraguayans deserve to know the truth,” he said. Peña is in pretrial detention on charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Prosecutors allege that he used his influence to steer public money to Ueno Bank, a lender used by more than half of Paraguay’s adults, as its executives made large insider loans to companies linked to the bank’s owners. The criminal association charge, added Friday, alleges that he led an organization that shielded Ueno from oversight. Peña denies wrongdoing. Paraguay’s central bank eventually seized Ueno on Nov. 3 after declaring it insolvent, freezing the accounts of nearly 3 million customers and more than $850 million in public funds, and disrupting payments for households and small businesses. Three days later, the Senate removed Peña from office, and Alliana took over. A judge ordered Peña jailed the next day. Ueno’s dizzying growth had become a symbol of Peña’s effort to sell landlocked Paraguay to foreign investors as a low-tax, business-friendly hub. A former International Monetary Fund official and one of the Trump administration’s closest allies in the region, Peña enjoyed prime access to Washington and Wall Street despite his country’s limited economic and geopolitical weight. The bank launched its digital brand in 2022 and by June had 2.9 million customers in a country of about 6 million. It even sponsored the national soccer team. But Ueno was also intertwined with Peña’s government. He held a stake in Ueno’s parent company until last year and appointed the bank’s former chairman, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank. Carvallo, who also faces charges in the case, has said through his lawyer that he did not take part in regulatory decisions involving Ueno. Since Peña’s arrest, authorities have searched two of his four homes, one in Asunción and a mansion in the resort town of San Bernardino, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) away. On Thursday, prosecutors also raided the presidential residence. Prosecutors say the mansion was built partly with about $577,000 in loans that Ueno granted Peña while he was president, and investigators found a vault hidden behind a false wall there. They have also asked the United States, Luxembourg and Argentina for help tracing money that may have been diverted from the bank. Alliana acknowledged that the crisis had shaken Paraguayans’ faith in their banks. “The closure of Ueno Bank has deeply affected numerous Paraguayan families,” he said. More than 1.8 million depositors have so far received about $640 million, Alliana said, from a deposit guarantee fund that Paraguay created in 2003 after a series of financial crises wiped out dozens of banks and finance companies. Most small savers have been repaid in full. The fund has paid out up to about $19,600 per person, out of a guarantee of about $36,700, and authorities haven’t said when the rest will be paid. Investors in Ueno’s mutual funds aren’t covered and must wait for the bank to be liquidated. Still, more than 75% of the roughly $2.8 billion deposited at Ueno, much of it belonging to larger savers and public institutions, has yet to be returned. For pension funds that had money at Ueno, Alliana said that authorities have preliminarily identified about $600 million in viable assets at the bank, such as loans expected to be repaid, that they plan to use to reimburse the funds. It remains unclear how much of the pension money and other public deposits will be returned. Teachers walked off the job and blocked roads across the country last week to demand the return of their retirement savings, and retirees’ groups have pressed Alliana and Congress to pass an emergency law to guarantee it. That followed days of unrest in Asunción after Ueno’s collapse, when thousands of people took to the streets demanding their money back and Peña’s ouster, at times clashing with police. DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina, and Nayara Batschke from Santiago, Chile.

articles.title: NYPD SRG disbanded: Mamdani, Tisch on NYC protest unit
articles.content: NEW YORK (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have agreed to disband the department's Strategic Response Group, or SRG, after months of discussions, officials announced Monday. "What we're doing today is announcing the disbanding of the Strategic Response Group and announcing a completely new approach to how we treat protest in our city," Mamdani told Eyewitness News in an exclusive joint interview with the NYPD Commissioner. The SRG is the NYPD's citywide rapid-deployment force that specializes in counterterrorism but also responds to major crimes and mass demonstrations. Critics have argued that the unit's crowd-control tactics are heavy-handed and provocative. Tisch said the SRG's 500 highly trained, uniformed officers will be reassigned, with many moving to the department's Counterterrorism Bureau. When asked whether the move represented a compromise, Tisch said, "No, I would never compromise on security for New Yorkers. And over the past year, we have made a number of massive changes in the department that strengthen our counterterrorism efforts, this among them." Mamdani said the city's new approach will focus on reducing tensions during demonstrations. "In addition to separating out those responsibilities, we're also emphasizing an approach of de-escalation, an approach of dialogue," he said. Over the next year, the city plans to hire and train civilians to work with protest organizers before and during demonstrations. Tisch said the change will not affect how the NYPD responds to civil disorder. "Nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions, like, for example, the celebrations following the Knicks' epic championship," Tisch said. "And so New Yorkers can expect in crowd control type situations to see the very same response that they are accustomed to." The commissioner had previously reduced the use of the SRG at protests while stopping short of disbanding the unit. The move fulfills a campaign promise made by the mayor. "He couldn't have been clearer about it, and he couldn't have been clearer about his interest in separating out First Amendment responsibility from counterterrorism responsibility. And that is something that I have long thought makes perfect sense. And so that's exactly what we've done here," Tisch said. "The reason we have taken 10 months to get to this point is to ensure that we could do so in a way that fulfilled the promise and was able to fulfill exactly those responsibilities that we hold," he said. "When you are in policing, you got to be proactive, not reactive. And that's what's not happening now. Now we're going backwards," said Scott Munro of the Detectives Endowment Association The unit is scheduled to be dissolved in the spring of next year, when a new NYPD crowd-control unit will assume responsibility for facilitating nonviolent protests.

articles.title: Introducing OpenAI for Chile
articles.description: OpenAI and the Government of Chile are partnering to support responsible AI adoption, build public-sector skills and help local startups develop AI applications.
articles.content: Today we’re launching OpenAI for Chile, a partnership with the Government of Chile, led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, to support responsible AI adoption in public administration, build civil servants’ skills and help local startups develop useful AI applications. The partnership builds on Chile’s National AI Policy and action plan(opens in a new window), which support talent development, research and responsible adoption. The Memorandum of Understanding was signed on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, with Minister Ximena Lincolao leading the agreement on behalf of Chile. The partnership is supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s American SI Exports Program(opens in a new window), of which OpenAI is an anchor partner, helping Chile advance its own AI ambitions through public sector innovation, skills development, and entrepreneurship. The partnership will explore technology adoption in the ministry’s administrative processes, including potential support from OpenAI on adopting new models, alongside advice and training for ministry personnel. For civil servants, the partnership will explore practical AI literacy, upskilling and reskilling tailored to their roles. Activities could include workshops and a train-the-trainer approach, covering effective use of AI tools, checking outputs, protecting sensitive information and maintaining human oversight. To support Chile’s AI startup and innovation ecosystem, the partners will explore access to relevant OpenAI programs and technology, practical learning, technical guidance and mentorship. Cooperation could also connect entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and other local partners to develop applications that support Chile’s economic development and public-service priorities. A joint task force of ministry and OpenAI representatives is expected to agree priorities and an initial workplan, with leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity. Specific activities, eligibility, resources and access to technology will be agreed separately. The MoU sets no investment or purchasing commitment. Activities will be subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use. OpenAI for Chile is part of OpenAI for Countries, our global initiative to help countries use AI to advance their national priorities, strengthen their economies and expand opportunity. We work with governments and local partners to turn AI’s potential into practical benefits for their people.

articles.title: Michigan's next attorney general plans departure from Washtenaw County Prosecutor's Office
articles.description: Eli Savit, recently elected as Michigan's next attorney general, says he plans to continue some of the litigation Dana Nessel has joined against the Trump administration.
articles.content: Michigan Democratic Attorney General candidate Eli Savit speaks to supporters on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026 at Hudson's Detroit. Savit defeated Republican Doug Lloyd in the AG race.(Zena Issa / Michigan Public )Michigan Attorney General-elect Eli Savit will step down as Washtenaw County prosecutor on December 4.Savit said he needs the extra time to catch up on pending litigation before his January 1 inauguration.“It really is a big operation, so we're going to be doing everything we can to make sure that we're not skipping a beat on day one,” Savit said.Most of the staff in the AG’s office is expected to stick around, he said.“The Attorney General is a political position,” said Savit. “But much of the work that the Attorney General's office does really is not political. It shouldn't depend on who's in charge. So there's dedicated civil servants there that have been there across multiple administrations.”Current Attorney General Dana Nessel has signed onto many lawsuits aimed at curbing Trump Administration policies. Savit plans to act similarly.“I have a simple two-part test for deciding whether to be involved in litigation against the federal government. Is what they're doing illegal, and does it harm the people of the state of Michigan? And if the answer to both those questions is yes, we'll see you in court,” Savit said.Victoria Burton-Harris, who served as Savit’s chief deputy in Washtenaw County, will take over as prosecutor in the interim.Savit said she is the right person to serve the final two years of his term, calling her a “tremendous leader, lawyer, and manager.”By law, a panel of Washtenaw County circuit court judges will decide who will finish out Savit’s term.

articles.title: Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months
articles.description: Three months since introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corba has raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.
articles.content: Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue. The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled. Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection. articles.title: Legal Roundup: What We Know About Lawsuits Council Discussed in a Closed-Door Meeting
articles.description: The council held a closed-door meeting with attorneys for almost four hours last week. Here's what they talked about.
articles.content: The East Lansing City Council had a special meeting Nov. 10, spending almost the entire four-hour session in a closed-door meeting with attorneys to discuss collective bargaining and pending lawsuits. The litigation discussed involves a police officer accused of causing a car crash while on duty, a dispute over the future cost of a downtown land lease, a developer challenging the City Council’s rejection of an apartment complex and two men who say they were wrongfully arrested and subjected to excessive force by police. East Lansing Info dug through court records to get the latest on the litigation the council discussed. Harrison v. City of East Lansing, East Lansing Police Department, and Logan Wainman This lawsuit was filed by Noel Harrison, who was injured after getting in a car accident with an East Lansing Police Department cruiser in April of 2024, according to filings at Ingham County’s 30th Circuit Court. According to filings, Harrison was driving north on Abbot Road near Lake Lansing Road. Harrison merged into the left hand turn lane when ELPD Officer Logan Wainman, who was traveling in the same direction, saw a speeding driver and began to make a U-turn without turning on emergency lights or signaling, crashing into Harrison’s car. According to Harrison’s attorneys, the collision caused spinal injuries that prevented her from sitting for long periods of time and living a normal life. In this litigation, East Lansing is represented by Giamarco, Mullins and Horton, the firm that held the city attorney contract at the time the litigation was filed. Attorney Anne Gabbert argued at a Feb. 25 hearing that Wainman’s actions did not meet the threshold of “gross negligence” and questioned the severity of Harrison’s injuries. While Harrison had healed by the time attorneys presented information in front of Circuit Court Judge Rosemarie Aquilina at the Feb. 25 hearing, the judge still saw the injuries as having an impact and said there is evidence Wainman was at fault for the accident. “She [Wainman] also admitted fault for the collision, as well as while I understand the defendants are arguing maybe negligence but not gross negligence, that is a question for the jury,” Aquilina said according to a transcript. “And gross negligence is defined as conduct so reckless as to demonstrate substantial lack of concern for whether an injury results, and I think a reasonable jury could make that conclusion.” There was a trial set for March 6, however, the city filed an appeal with the Michigan Appellate Court regarding government immunity and at the Feb. 25 hearing, Aquilina said that trial was adjourned to let the appeal play out. The appeal was dismissed in September, according to the Michigan Appellate court’s website. TDP Acquisitions, LLC v. City of East Lansing This litigation was initiated in August, shortly after the East Lansing City Council rejected a 10-story apartment complex proposed by Tareen Development Partners, or TDP, where the Bailey Street surface parking lot currently sits. As ELi previously reported, TDP is asking an Ingham County 30th Circuit Court judge to overturn the council’s decision, writing in an appeal that the city’s site plan review was unnecessary and broke the law. TDP’s attorneys argued that the proposed development met the city’s zoning standards and therefore would only need to receive a building permit. The City Council rejected the apartment at a July 21 meeting, citing concerns about the proposal’s compatibility with nearby properties, parking and traffic congestion. The council also raised concerns about a heating and cooling system planned for the project that city staff members said could harm an important aquifer, however, developers offered to drop this portion of the project at the July meeting. In a court filing, TDP’s attorneys called the decision to reject the apartment “arbitrary and capricious.” Along with asking the court to overturn the council’s decision and allow the development to proceed, TDP is asking for attorney fees and other costs incurred during the appeals process, according to filings. While the litigation is still in early stages, more recent filings show that the City Council’s approval of “The Howard” will be part of TDP’s argument. The Howard is a 12-story apartment being constructed downtown that was approved at the same meeting TDP’s project was rejected. Along with asking for notes and other materials related to the council’s decision to reject TDP’s apartment, the developer’s attorneys are asking for materials related to the approval of The Howard. In its most recent filing, submitted Nov. 10, the city asked the court to limit the record to materials considered by the City Council at its July 21 meeting and the development’s site plan. City attorneys argued that documents related to The Howard and minutes from city board and commission meetings should be excluded because they were not part of the council’s decision. University Place Condominium Associates v. City of East Lansing For 40 years, University Place Associates Condominium Association has leased the property that hosts the Marriott Hotel, a parking garage and several businesses for just $10 per year, developing the land and building the parking garage in exchange for the minuscule rate. In April, ELi reported that University Place is suing East Lansing over a dispute about the terms of its future lease, including how much it will pay. The city has countersued. The litigation is pending in Ingham County Circuit Court. The original agreement stipulated University Place could renew its lease in 10-year increments for annual payments equal to 12% of the land value, which could push the $10 lease payments to more than $500,000 annually. Now, there is a disagreement about the new lease amount. In 2019, the city and University Place each had the land assessed, with the city’s assessment finding a value of $4.1 million and University Place’s assessment finding a value of $3.1 million. With the wide disparity in valuations, a third assessment was done. The third assessment valued the property at $4.5 million. The city claims that the value of the land would be determined by taking the average of the third valuation and the assessment closest to it, a methodology city attorneys say University Place participated in implementing. This would make the value about $4.35 million and annual payments about $520,000. However, University Place lawyers argue in filings that the Marriott Hotel’s lender, Huntington National Bank, was not involved in the assessment process. Lawyers say Huntington had to be included according to an estoppel agreement the city and Marriott entered in 2016. The city has accused University Place of “stringing [it] along” for years and disputing a land appraisal process it participated in, filing a countersuit. The latest filings, entered to the Circuit Court on May 19, show the value of the land is still being contested. Smith and Woods v. City of East Lansing et al This litigation was filed in the U.S. Western District Court of Michigan in Grand Rapids and has gained significant attention over the last year. In August of 2025, during Michigan State University’s Welcome Weekend, an ELPD officer pepper-sprayed two young Black men downtown. The department issued a press release about violence downtown that singled the two men pepper-sprayed out by name, Lonnie Smith and Mason Woods, stating that they were arrested for charges related to fighting. However, the attorney for both men, Jack Rucker, later released security footage from a business that appears to show Smith stepped in to deescalate an altercation between his friend Woods and other men in line outside of a restaurant. After the footage was made public, city attorneys dropped charges against both men. It was extremely unusual for the city to include the names of individuals accused of misdemeanors in a press release. A series of records requests by East Lansing Info showed that prior to the press release’s publication, the city’s communications consultants believed they were to include another individual arrested for unrelated reasons because he shares a last name with Smith’s mother, Nadia Sellers. For weeks prior to the press release’s publication, Sellers had been speaking critically about the police department at city meetings. Despite substantial public interest, city officials have declined to comment on the incident for more than a year, saying that speaking on the matter could jeopardize the city’s insurance coverage. In an email to ELi, Rucker said there has been little recent movement in the case, with about 15 depositions scheduled for December and January. He added that he hopes to see progress on discovery requests after filing a motion to compel last month. Do you have a question that you would like ELi to investigate? Just click here! articles.title: Trump clipped Biden's payouts for stranded travelers. It may not have helped during the ground stop
articles.description: Trump clipped Biden's payouts for stranded travelers. It may not have helped during the ground stop AP News ‘It’s life’: Trump brushes aside concerns about outages NBC News Seth Meyers responds to Trump's 'I don’t take any responsibility' stance on FAA ground stop Mashable As Crisis Circled the Skies, Trump Kept Out of Sight and Off Topic The New York Times Trump on tech outages: 'It's fine' Yahoo
articles.content: President Donald Trump has blamed the nationwide grounding of all planes last week on old technology, as well as on his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden. Trump’s administration weakened Biden-era rules to help stranded travelers — though it would not likely have helped many after Friday’s FAA-ordered ground stop. That remuneration was tied to issues with the airlines themselves. And officials have said that the disruption that marooned thousands of travelers and led to cascading flight issues that bled into the new week resulted from a router issue in the aging air traffic control system — not with the airlines. Here’s a look at what the Biden administration proposed to help alleviate travelers’ stress, and Trump’s subsequent actions: In its closing days at the end of 2024, the Biden administration took steps toward requiring airlines to pay cash and cover lodging and meals for stranded passengers. Awards started at $200, with compensation as high as $775 proposed for delays of nine hours or more. The rule went far beyond requirements for airlines to pay ticket refunds, putting U.S. policy more closely in line with airline consumer protections in Europe. But the mechanism also hinged on issues with the airlines, not agencies like the FAA; flight cancellations or significant delays needed to originate with a mechanical problem with the plane or an airline computer outage. Following last week’s ground stop, airlines largely waived rebooking fees for travelers seeking another flight and offered travel credits for use on a future flight. There were not blanket reimbursements offered for hotel and meal costs, not to mention the costs incurred for renting a car or somehow finding alternate travel. Last year, the Trump administration announced it was abandoning the plan, calling the reversal “consistent with Department and administration priorities.” Under Secretary Sean Duffy, DOT formally withdrew its airline passenger-rights proposal a year ago, citing Trump’s directives aimed at reducing private companies’ financial burden to comply with regulations. Industry trade group Airlines for America, which represents carriers including United, Delta and Southwest Airlines, welcomed the move by the Trump administration. Airlines already offer some level of customer service when they cause flight cancellations or severe delays, but passengers usually have to ask for help at the airport, and airline promises don’t carry the weight of federal rules. Thanks to a separate measure introduced in the Biden administration, airlines do have to give cash refunds but only when certain conditions are met, like if a flight is canceled and a passenger doesn’t want to take a rebooked trip. A passenger would also be entitled to a refund if a domestic flight were delayed more than three hours, and they opted not to continue the trip. Trump volleys back to Congress in blame game over aviation ground stop
articles.description: President Donald Trump on Monday accused Congress of underfunding the nation’s aviation infrastructure, which he blamed for the weekend ground stop that caused thousands of canceled and delayed flights. But Democrats say the Trump administration has been slow to spend already appropriated funds and decisions made by the administration have harmed the Department of Transportation. […]
articles.content: A jet flies over Washington, D.C., on May 5, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)President Donald Trump on Monday accused Congress of underfunding the nation’s aviation infrastructure, which he blamed for the weekend ground stop that caused thousands of canceled and delayed flights. But Democrats say the Trump administration has been slow to spend already appropriated funds and decisions made by the administration have harmed the Department of Transportation. Congress controls federal funding levels, and Trump predicted during informal remarks to reporters before departing on an overseas trip that lawmakers would soon pay to overhaul the air traffic control system after a communications failure froze air travel for hours Friday night. Air traffic control should have been updated 40 years ago, he added. “I think the one good thing that comes out of it, I’m sure Congress now will give us the money to pay” for it, he said. Dems say few answers But the amount of funding has not been an obstacle to Federal Aviation Administration improvements, top U.S. House Democratic appropriators said Sunday. Their pushback followed a Friday night press conference from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that the Democrats said provided few answers about the cause of the disruption. Duffy asked for $50 billion in new spending to upgrade air traffic control infrastructure during the press conference. But the Transportation Department and FAA have failed to spend more than $9 billion of the $12.5 billion the Republican-controlled Congress provided last year, House Appropriations Committee ranking member Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut wrote in a press release Sunday. “Instead of laying out the facts, Secretary Duffy commanded the public’s attention to demand a $50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver,” DeLauro wrote. Rep. Jim Clyburn, a South Carolina Democrat who is the ranking member of the Appropriations subcommittee that writes the Transportation Department’s annual funding bill, said Duffy would have to make a more persuasive case to win any new funding. “Recent events are not the result of a lack of funding or support from this Congress,” Clyburn said in the same release. “They result from leadership decisions that continue to put politics and private interests above the public’s interests.” Monday afternoon, the Senate Appropriations Committee released its bill to fund the Transportation Department for the coming fiscal year. The measure includes $4.5 billion for air traffic control modernization — a $500 million boost compared to what the White House sought in its annual budget request, but well below Duffy’s more recent ask. In a statement, subcommittee Chair Cindy Hyde-Smith noted that “recent incidents show us the importance of investments included in this important legislation.” The bill “provides funding to continue air traffic control modernization and the hiring of controllers, while also providing resources to improve our nation’s bridges, roads, ports, and shipyards,” she added. Spokespeople for the Transportation Department and FAA did not respond to requests for comment Monday. Disrupted travel The ground stop, which lasted for about five hours Friday afternoon and evening, meant all planes departing or arriving in the United States could not take off. Nearly 10,000 major commercial airline flights were canceled. The FAA said it issued the groundstop after a failure in its communications system. New equipment operating on old infrastructure at an El Dorado, Arkansas, radio communications facility malfunctioned and overwhelmed the system. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, also sent faulty data, the FAA said in a Q&A posted Sunday. “L3 Harris, the FAA’s current network service provider, had been doing work at the El Dorado site, including deployment of a new router,” the FAA Q&A said. “When these inconsistencies in the data happened, L3 Harris blocked those two locations and the network stabilized. The broadcasting function was also disabled on all the new routers as a precaution.” Longtime issue Nearly two years after Trump’s return to the White House, he also blamed his predecessor, President Joe Biden, Monday for the shutdown that was caused by a communications failure. But Trump also said the issue was decades in the making, with many air traffic control assets 50 years old. The rollout of a massive, multi-decade, roughly $13-billion initiative to overhaul the air traffic control system routinely received criticism from across the political spectrum for being behind schedule and over-budget. The program, known as NextGen, was shuttered in 2025 and the FAA folded its general “modernization” mission into other offices.

Americans increasingly see crime declining, but fears of scams persist, survey finds
articles.description: Americans are increasingly optimistic about the nation’s crime trends, with perceptions of rising crime hovering near historic lows even as nearly half the country still believes crime is getting worse, according to a new Gallup poll. Forty-six percent of U.S. adults say crime has increased nationally over the past year, down sharply from 77% in […]
articles.content: Members of the New York Police Department bomb squad and agents with the FBI conduct a criminal investigation in New York City. Americans’ perceptions of rising crime are near historic lows, according to a new Gallup poll, even as concerns about financial scams and identity theft persist. (Photo by Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)Americans are increasingly optimistic about the nation’s crime trends, with perceptions of rising crime hovering near historic lows even as nearly half the country still believes crime is getting worse, according to a new Gallup poll. Forty-six percent of U.S. adults say crime has increased nationally over the past year, down sharply from 77% in 2023 and little changed from 49% last year. The figure has been lower only once since Gallup began tracking national perceptions in 1989. Americans are even less likely to believe crime is rising in their own communities. About a third, 33%, say local crime has increased over the past year, among the lowest readings in more than five decades of polling. The findings, based on an Oct. 1-19 survey, come as federal crime statistics show substantial declines in violence across the country. National crime data released earlier this year by the FBI showed violent crime fell 9.3% in 2025 from the previous year, the largest annual drop since the agency began tracking national estimates in 1936. The murder rate also plunged 18.5% to 4.1 killings per 100,000 people, tying its lowest recorded level in nearly 90 years. The rate matches those recorded in 1955 and 1956. The decline extends beyond crimes reported to police. Preliminary findings from the federal Bureau of Justice Statistics’ National Crime Victimization Survey, which captures nonfatal crimes whether or not they were reported to law enforcement, showed that violent victimization, excluding simple assault, fell 25% in 2025. Aggravated assaults dropped 31%, while robberies declined 27%. Still, Americans’ perceptions of crime have not entirely caught up with those trends. The divide between national and local perceptions has persisted for decades, with Americans consistently more likely to believe crime is increasing across the country than to think it’s rising in their own neighborhoods. That gap has narrowed considerably in recent years. In 2022, a record 56% of Americans said crime was rising locally, compared with 33% today. Political differences also have diminished. Just two years ago, Republicans and Democrats were sharply divided over whether national crime was increasing. Those differences narrowed last year, and Republicans’ perceptions of rising national crime fell another 15 percentage points in the latest survey. The poll also highlights a shift in what Americans fear most: Financial crimes continue to generate considerably more concern than violent offenses. Seven in 10 Americans say they worry at least occasionally about becoming victims of identity theft, while 55% worry about being tricked by scammers into sending money or providing access to their financial accounts. Those were the only two offenses among 10 surveyed that worried a majority of respondents. By comparison, 41% worry about having their vehicle stolen or broken into, while the same share worry about a school-age child being physically harmed at school. About 37% fear a home burglary, and 22% worry about being murdered. Concerns also vary considerably by age, income and gender. Older Americans are particularly worried about financial crimes. Among adults 55 and older, 77% express concern about identity theft, compared with 52% of adults younger than 35. Younger adults, meanwhile, report greater concern about most violent crimes. Women are also more likely than men to worry about all eight nonfinancial crimes surveyed, including sexual assault, which worries 40% of women compared with 13% of men. Lower-income Americans consistently express greater concern about violent crime than higher-income adults. Nearly a third of adults earning less than $50,000 annually worry about being murdered, compared with 13% of those earning at least $100,000. Although fears surrounding many crimes have eased from their recent peaks in 2022 and 2023, concerns about hate crimes, school violence and identity theft remain elevated. Worry about sexual assault also increased over the past year. The findings underscore a persistent disconnect between improving national crime statistics and Americans’ concerns about their personal safety, particularly as financial fraud and certain forms of violence continue to weigh heavily on the public. articles.title: New World screwworm spreading rapidly across Southwestern states
articles.description: A deadly flesh-eating parasite that can plague livestock, wildlife and pets continues to spread across the American Southwest. Officials detected the arrival of the New World screwworm in June — the first time in decades the pest had been seen in the United States. Since then, detections have spiked, with 139 recorded cases across three […]
articles.content: A pinned specimen of a full-grown New World screwworm fly is shown in this image. Federal and state officials are grappling with a worsening infestation from the flesh-eating parasite that threatens livestock, pets and wildlife. (Photo courtesy of Michael Miller/Texas A&M AgriLife)A deadly flesh-eating parasite that can plague livestock, wildlife and pets continues to spread across the American Southwest. Officials detected the arrival of the New World screwworm in June — the first time in decades the pest had been seen in the United States. Since then, detections have spiked, with 139 recorded cases across three states. While fewer than 10 total cases were recorded in August and September, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has already confirmed 53 cases this month. “We got a bunch more cases all of a sudden,” said David Anderson, professor and extension economist in livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University. Rising infections have pushed state leaders to designate certain outbreak areas across Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, where animal movement is being restricted. The movement of pets and livestock is restricted in all or parts of 31 Texas counties as officials there are tracking 77 sites with at least one confirmed case. Contrary to its name, the screwworm grows into an adult fly about the size of a common housefly. The name screwworm refers to the larvae (maggots) that burrow into open wounds, feeding as they go “like a screw being driven into wood,” according to USDA. The pest could threaten beef and dairy cattle — potentially exacerbating high prices for consumers. But the screwworm can also infect people, wildlife and pets. That’s pushed states to recommend or require certain monitoring of pet movements. California, for instance, requires all warm-blooded animals coming from an infested zone to have a pretravel inspection, a veterinary certification and an entry permit into the state. In Texas, adoptions for thousands of dogs and cats were put on hold in August as most states restricted movement of animals from areas with screwworm infestations. “It’s thrown a wrench into things, for small rescues as well as the bigger shelters,” Mia Bendixsen, executive director of the Texas Humane Legislation Network, told The Associated Press. Earlier this month, the New Mexico Livestock Board broadened its screwworm tracking to regional infestation zones as more cases were confirmed across southern parts of the state. Those zones demarcate where ranchers must receive state authorization before moving cattle. “We are working closely with our state and federal partners to investigate these cases, increase surveillance and monitor for additional infestations,” New Mexico State Veterinarian Samantha Holeck said in an October statement, according to Source New Mexico. Screwworm maggots burrow into the flesh of living animals through wounds as small as a tick bite or in body openings such as the eyes or nose. That means ranchers must keep close watch over newborn calves with exposed umbilical cords and may need to rethink branding and tagging operations that provide an entry for the pests. While the flies could prove deadly to herds, USDA says they do not create food safety risks. But a worsening infestation could impact beef prices, which are already near record high prices. In August, federal officials began a phased reopening of Southern ports for cattle imports from Mexico, which had been barred because of the screwworm infestation. That should slowly help rebuild the domestic cattle supply chain and eventually offer some relief for consumers, said Anderson, of Texas A&M. Much of southern New Mexico a designated screwworm ‘infested zone’ as USDA reopens cattle imports Anderson expects consumers could see some relief in prices next year. But grocery shoppers shouldn’t expect a return to the rock-bottom beef prices they enjoyed five to 10 years ago. “Because there’s so many other costs, not only producing and processing the animals, but transportation, labor — everything is higher,” he said. The screwworm can infect humans, but so far no domestic cases have been reported in people, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Mexico and Central American nations have reported more than 2,850 cases in people, according to CDC tracking. To eradicate the pests, the federal government plans to breed sterile male flies and then release them into areas with established populations. The sterilized males will mate with females, which will then lay unfertilized eggs. With females mating only once in their lifespan, officials say this method progressively reduces and eliminates the fly population. USDA is constructing a $750 million sterile fly facility in Southern Texas that aims to produce up to 300 million sterile flies per week when it opens next year. The agency has also invested in sterile fly facilities in Mexico and Panama. Last week, the federal government began the process of hiring 228 people for the new Texas facility. “Protecting U.S. livestock and wildlife from New World Screwworm is a national security priority, and this new facility will drastically boost the availability of sterile flies – our most successful offensive capability to drive these serious pests away from our border,” Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said in a news release about the hiring. articles.title: NAC members: ‘No reason to delay’ RenCen benefits agreement
articles.description: "It isn’t a loan to be paid back to the city. It is an investment – by the Michigan Strategic Fund - to save, arguably, Detroit’s most iconic building."
articles.content: In response to the Nov. 14 opinion piece entitled We should delay GM, Bedrock’s plans for Detroit’s Riverfront, we want to clarify misconceptions about the Community Benefits Ordinance process and the proposed agreement before the Detroit City Council. The piece was written by the only Renaissance Center/East Riverfront Neighborhood Advisory Committee (NAC) member who voted against our historic community benefits agreement. The NAC had many marathon work sessions lasting more than eight to 10 hours, and we went into the process knowing that. We made a commitment to participate because Detroit and Detroiters deserved such an effort. With our mission to serve our city as our only motivation, none of us were intimidated by those we sat across the table from in negotiations. The city of Detroit’s Planning Department, which was present at every marathon meeting, did an amazing job providing policy support where needed, as well as making the entire administration and its subject matter experts available to us upon request. As the NAC, our assignment was simple and practical: negotiate a community impact and benefits agreement on behalf of Detroiters. That was our focus. Our assignment was never to reject or reshape this project. Nor was it to focus on development timelines, construction or operational costs. As the NAC, we never believed public transit was the responsibility of this developer. We all saw public transit as an issue for local, state and federal government to address. The city agreed with us. We understand the $300 million commitment to this project isn’t a “blank check” to developers or a “check” at all. And it isn’t a loan to be paid back to the city. It is an investment – by the Michigan Strategic Fund – to save, arguably, Detroit’s most iconic building. The $174 million in tax abatements isn’t a “check” either. It’s simply a discount on future taxes that not only do not currently exist today but will never exist if this project isn’t built. And above all, we understand the developer gets none of these financial commitments if the project is not completed and operating at projected levels. We understand the “taxes” from this project were never going to be withdrawn from or deposited into the city’s general fund. Whether the developer received tax incentives or not, the taxes from this project would/will be collected by the Downtown Development Authority, not the city – by law. We understand that technically, the city’s only role in this process is to evaluate and approve this project to allow the state to invest the funds into the RenCen development, while leveraging this economic opportunity to create both construction and permanent jobs for Detroiters, affordable housing, neighborhood investment, workforce training and Detroit-based business inclusion for Detroit residents, among other things. Therefore, we see the risk of this project differently than our sole colleague. What we consider at risk is an investor willing to make a $1.6 billion investment to reimagine the Renaissance Center; a half billion-dollar investment to Detroit by the Michigan Strategic Fund; a $95 million up front payment to the city to be used immediately to improve city services; an extra $300 million to the city over the course of construction period to do the same; the $113 million in community benefits (including $43.5 million in direct monetary benefits) that we negotiated in our agreement; and the more than $3 billion in economic activity that Detroit will enjoy for years to come after this project is complete. Let us be clear: None of this takes place without this project. Therefore, we, the undersigned members of the Neighborhood Advisory Council, not only stand by the historic community benefits agreement that we negotiated; we see no reason to delay this project from moving forward. Editor’s note: This story was written by Jamaine Dickens, the chair of the NAC, on behalf of the board, which includes Bernard Morgan II, Vice Chair; Jeff Mastej, Parliamentarian; Deirdre Jackson; Gail Perry Mason; Linda Middlebrooks Talbot; Aloshia Jackson; and Patrice Woodard. All members listed signed off. Jamaine Dickens is the principal of Compass Strategies, a public affairs firm in Detroit. He is the former spokesperson for the City of Detroit, and former communications director for the Michigan Legislature. He is currently serving as the chair of the Neighborhood Advisory Council for the Renaissance Center/East Riverfront project.

articles.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365

articles.content: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. Defying court order, Trump admin again forces Michigan coal plant to stay open
articles.description: The Energy Department has again extended an order forcing an aging Michigan coal-fired power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date, defying a order by a three-judge panel that set aside the agency’s previous actions.
articles.content: WASHINGTON — The Energy Department has again extended an order forcing an aging Michigan coal-fired power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date, defying a court order that set aside the agency’s previous actions as unlawful. Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued an emergency order late Friday extending the continued operation of the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell Generating Plant near Grand Rapids, saying the plant is needed to prevent blackouts and preserve customers’ access to reliable, secure electricity. The Energy Department said it disagrees with the September decision by a three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and has petitioned for a rehearing in front of the entire court. The emergency order is among a series of actions by President Donald Trump and his administration to boost the struggling U.S. coal industry, including a plan announced in June to spend nearly $700 million to support coal-fired power plants and coal exports. The Environmental Protection Agency, meanwhile, has repealed rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The agency under Administrator Lee Zeldin also is moving to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants. Related: Court strikes Trump order that forced Michigan coal plant to stay open Trump administration extends order to keep Michigan coal plant open Trump admin cancels $156M Michigan solar program as coal plant decision looms Michigan coal plant’s future unclear as some wonder if feds will keep it open Environmental groups slammed the latest emergency order on coal — the seventh such declaration for the Campbell plant since May 2025 — and said there is no evidence that the Michigan plant has ever been needed to avoid a grid emergency or prevented power outages. Opinon: Detroit should take this opportunity to reimagine the Renaissance Center
articles.description: The riverfront should not feel separated from the city it represents. The Bedrock proposal offers an opportunity to address those mistakes.
articles.content: As someone who plans to begin limiting my civic engagement, I want to make one final contribution to an important conversation about the future of Detroit before I do. That conversation is about the future of the Renaissance Center. I support General Motors Co. and Bedrock’s proposal to redesign, re-envision, and reimagine the Renaissance Center, and I believe Detroit City Council should give serious consideration to approving the proposal. I say that with a deep appreciation for what the Renaissance Center has represented throughout my lifetime. When the complex was built under the leadership of Henry Ford II, it represented something complicated. To me, it symbolized both the good and the bad — a fresh start for a city searching for renewal but also a new form of isolation rather than the segregation we had known before. History gives us many things whose meaning we cannot change. The Renaissance Center is different. We have an opportunity to influence what this landmark represents in the future. We can help make the RenCen a symbol not of isolation, but of a sustainable Detroit Renaissance. We cannot let the RenCen become a ruin. Horace Sheffield The Renaissance Center is one of Detroit’s most recognizable images. It is part of the city’s postcard, skyline and identity. We cannot allow it to become another Packard Plant — a monument to what Detroit once was rather than a place that helps define what Detroit can become. The Renaissance Center has to change if it is going to survive. But change does not have to mean abandoning Detroit’s history. It can mean preserving what is worth preserving while correcting what never worked. The iconic skyline can remain while the property takes on a new purpose. For too long, the Renaissance Center has functioned as a confusing fortress. Detroiters know it. Visitors experience it. The riverfront should not feel separated from the city it represents. The Bedrock proposal offers an opportunity to address those mistakes. By opening the complex and making it more inviting, accessible, and inclusive — including through new affordable housing — we can begin to reconnect the RenCen with Detroit and with Detroiters. Another important part of the proposal is the transformation of approximately 35 acres of empty surface parking lots into a family-friendly entertainment district. That is the kind of opportunity Detroit should embrace. Our city deserves the kinds of experiences and attractions that residents and visitors find in other major American cities. Chicago’s Navy Pier is one example of how a waterfront can become a destination for families, residents and visitors. Detroit should be able to create its own version of that experience — one rooted in our own history, culture, architecture, music, food and character. Our riverfront is one of our greatest assets. We should continue finding ways to make it more accessible and create more opportunities for people to gather, celebrate and experience the best of Detroit. The incentives deserve a factual discussion. There has, understandably, been discussion about the proposed incentives, and that discussion should continue. But the facts matter. According to the city’s analysis, this development is not being undertaken as a profit-making venture. Under the proposed structure, the city is projected to receive approximately $300 million in new tax revenue. That figure deserves to be considered in the broader context of what Detroit is trying to accomplish. A nonprofit development structure involving Bedrock and GM, coupled with projected new tax revenue for the city, represents an opportunity to transform one of Detroit’s most recognizable landmarks while creating a new economic and civic purpose for the property. This is not simply about a building. It is about what kind of city Detroit wants to be. The Renaissance Center has already played an important role in Detroit’s story. Now we have an opportunity to determine what role it will play in the next chapter. We should not be afraid of change simply because the building is iconic. We should ask whether we can preserve its importance while making it more open, useful, welcoming and connected to the city around it. I believe we can. And I believe this opportunity deserves our support. Detroit has a chance to do more than preserve the Renaissance Center. We have a chance to redefine what it represents for generations to come. Rev. Horace L. Sheffield III is pastor of New Destiny Church and a third-generation Detroiter. He is also the father of Mayor Mary Sheffield.

articles.title: More countries have antimicrobial resistance plans but patients still lack testing and treatment
articles.content: As more countries are taking steps to tackle antimicrobial resistance (AMR), major gaps that remain in testing and treatment mean that many patients are still at risk, according to new data from the World Health Organization (WHO). When medicines lose their effectiveness against resistant bacteria and other microbes, common infections become harder to treat and routine medical procedures, including surgery, childbirth and cancer care, become riskier. In 2023, approximately 1 in 6 laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide were resistant to antibiotics, highlighting the growing threat to patients. The new findings released today ahead of World AMR Awareness Week, show that 173 countries report having developed plans to address AMR, more than double the 79 countries that reported doing so in 2017. But having a plan does not necessarily mean patients are protected. Only 22% of countries report having both the necessary funding and full implementation of national AMR action plans. This leaves major gaps worldwide along the pathway of care, from preventing infections to diagnosing and treating patients, as well as detecting resistance trends and taking control measures. “National plans are essential for protecting the medicines that protect us, and the fact that most countries now have plans in place is great news," said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. "But an unfulfilled plan helps no one. We call on all countries to implement their plans with investments in infection prevention, surveillance, equitable access to essential antimicrobials and quality diagnostics. Every infection prevented means fewer antimicrobials are needed, and testing ensures that patients receive the right treatment only when necessary. The findings are included in the latest Tracking Antimicrobial Resistance Country Self-assessment Survey (TrACSS), completed by 183 countries (94% of Member States) in 2026. Access to diagnostic testing helps ensure patients receive the right treatment at the right time. However, such testing is inadequate in most countries. Only 36% of countries report having a national reference laboratory equipped to test the selected bacteria and fungi. This falls far short of the global target of 80% of countries having comprehensive bacterial and fungal resistance testing capacity by 2030. Inadequate access to diagnostic tests increases the risk of patients being prescribed antibiotics that are ineffective or unnecessary. Resistant infections and outbreaks may go undetected, while gaps in surveillance data limit understanding of local resistance patterns. The gaps extend further to treatment guidelines and surveillance. Only 63% of countries report having guidelines on appropriate use of antimicrobials, and just over half report having surveillance systems to monitor national antibiotic use and track levels of AMR. To help countries close the gaps, WHO released two new practical tools as part of the AMR Diagnostic Initiative. The tools provide a prioritized catalogue of diagnostic tests and step-by-step methods to help clinical laboratories diagnose bacterial and fungal infections. World AMR Awareness Week, held 18–24 November, is a global campaign to raise awareness of AMR and promote action to prevent the emergence and spread of drug-resistant infections. Under the 2026 theme, “One Health, one action: Prevent AMR now”, the campaign highlights the interconnected health of people, animals, plants and the environment, and calls on everyone – from governments to farmers, veterinarians, environmental experts and communities – to take action to prevent AMR. Established in 2016, the Tracking Antimicrobial Resistance Country Self-assessment Survey (TrACSS) is the only global mechanism monitoring how countries implement their national actions on AMR. Developed by the Quadripartite organizations FAO, UNEP, WHO and WOAH, the annual self-assessment provides a comprehensive picture of country progress and informs monitoring of commitments under the 2024 UN General Assembly Political Declaration on AMR. Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide.
