articles.title: New York Mayor Mamdani disbands 'notorious' police unit that used excessive force on protesters
articles.content: NEW YORK, Nov 16 (Reuters) - New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is disbanding a police unit criticized for using excessive force against protesters in favor of a new "civilian-led approach" to large public demonstrations, he announced on Monday. Mamdani promised in his election campaign last year to disband the police department's Strategic Response Group, a decade-old anti-terrorism unit that has faced legal challenges for its rough tactics at street protests, including the use of pepper spray by armed officers in riot gear and mass arrests. In the joint announcement alongside New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, Mamdani said he is creating a new civilian-led group called the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, whose members would be unarmed and would not have arrest powers. At the New York Police Department, he said the disbanded SRG unit would be replaced in part by a new unit called the Patrol Support Division, which he said would police protests differently. "New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," the mayor said in a statement. The SRG was rebuked in a 2023 legal settlement after New York Attorney General Letitia James, the New York Civil Liberties Union and others sued over excessive force against protesters, journalists and legal observers during protests against police violence in the summer of 2020. The NYCLU and other civil rights groups cautiously welcomed Mamdani's announcement, while expressing concern that the new Patrol Support Division might end up a rebranding of the SRG, not a disbanding. The Legal Aid Society, the city's largest public defender's office, on Monday commended the disbanding of "one of the NYPD's most notorious units" in a statement, but said the new unit "will require vigilant oversight to ensure that the SRG's tactics are not repeated." The NYCLU said it will be "monitoring this new unit closely, including for compliance with our 2023 settlement with the City." Tisch, who runs one of the world's largest police forces and its nearly $7 billion annual operating budget, said there were about 500 SRG officers who would be reassigned within the department before next spring. Some, she added, would go to the existing Counterterrorism Bureau. "Nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions," Tisch told ABC's Eyewitness News in a joint interview with the mayor. A spokesperson for the mayor did not respond to queries about how the new Patrol Support Division would differ from the SRG, or whether it would be staffed by former SRG officers. Police unions criticized the move, saying it would endanger the safety of officers and the public. "The next time your life is disrupted by demonstrators who are blocking bridges and roadways or causing chaos on our streets, remember: Mayor Mamdani is on their side, not yours," Patrick Hendry, president of the Police Benevolent Association, said in a statement. articles.title: California Sues OpenAI Over A.I. Safety Issues
articles.description: The state attorney general filed a lawsuit accusing the company of failing to put appropriate safeguards on its artificial intelligence and putting the public at risk.
articles.content: The state attorney general filed a lawsuit accusing the company of failing to put appropriate safeguards on its artificial intelligence and putting the public at risk. California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the company of putting the public at risk by failing to put appropriate safeguards on its artificial intelligence. The lawsuit is the latest broadside at the company, which — along with other tech industry players — has faced scrutiny over a rush to develop A.I. at the potential expense of consumer safety. In a 31-page lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, the state said OpenAI’s lax safeguards led to cyberattacks by its A.I. products during testing, including a breach this year when OpenAI’s agents went rogue and attacked the A.I. start-up Hugging Face’s systems. OpenAI’s behavior created a public nuisance and violated a legal prohibition on unfair or fraudulent business practices, the state said. “OpenAI’s failure to adequately secure and monitor the testing of its highly capable and increasingly powerful A.I. models represents a danger to the public that must be remedied,” the state said in the lawsuit. The move is the latest effort by a state to rein in the power of A.I. companies in the face of growing concerns about the technology’s ability to go rogue. In recent months, A.I. systems produced by major companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have broken out of testing environments designed to keep them from launching cyberattacks on companies and governments, raising alarms. Courts must still decide how legal liability will be applied in those cases. But there are growing calls for developers of powerful A.I. systems to be held responsible when those systems behave unexpectedly. We are having trouble retrieving the article content. articles.description: Two years after its inception, the clinic helps 500 women a year get medical screenings while providing them with health education, mental health services and more The post Zaman Community Health Center offers marginalized women alternative healthcare options appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: Two years after its inception, the clinic helps 500 women a year get medical screenings while providing them with health education, mental health services and more Two years ago, the Inkster-based nonprofit Zaman International opened the Zaman Community Health Center to expand client services. Zaman International works to uplift marginalized women and children to break the cycles of poverty, for women whose income is at or below $15,000. Eman Hazimi, Director of Health Services, says the center was added as part of Founder Najah Bazzi’s hope to expand basic needs. “With her nursing background, she felt that health should be included,” she says. Hazimi is also a nurse practitioner by trade. The center provides medical, mental health, health screenings and educational classes, free to 500 women a year. “We service both insured, uninsured, and actually recently we’ve been serving a lot of underinsured patients… who just cannot afford their copays, cannot afford their medications, their office visits,” she says. Hazimi says the staff is mostly bilingual, serving mostly an Arabic-speaking client base. The center also has interpreters on hand. Services include a comprehensive physical workup and prevention services, including breast and cervical cancer screenings through a partnership with the state of Michigan and the Breast and Cervical Cancer Control Navigation Program (BC3NP), which offers free screenings and follow-up care for low-income women. “We keep a tracker so that way we can make sure we do yearly checkups,” she says. The health center has six paid staff and several volunteers. The center also provides health education workshops for emotional wellness support, chronic disease management and parenting classes. Another offering is mental health services through a licensed behavioral therapist. “A lot of our clients have been through PTSD, they’ve been through domestic violence issues… a lot of them have to have been displaced or immigrated, so this is a whole new world for them, and they’re starting all over, and that takes a toll on them,” she explains. The community center does not take patients outside of their immediate clients at this time. To find out more about the Zaman Community Health Center, contact 313-710-1112 between 9 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. Monday through Friday.

articles.content: (Stock photo/Getty Images)Michigan’s largest teachers’ union will be looking to the incoming Democratic legislative majority and the state’s new governor to help educators find solutions to poor student behavior in the classroom, which the Michigan Education Association said could be addressed through a potential mix of pilot programs, appropriations and other solutions identified during a recent news conference. Last week, the MEA presented new data from a survey of more than 4,000 members involved in preK-12 education, conducted Aug. 12-21, 2026. The MEA found that members continue to face challenges with student behavior and that almost all of the respondents surveyed reported at least one negative student behavior experience within the last year. The share of members concerned about student violence toward other students or employees has also risen, the data notes. Of the key findings, almost half of members surveyed experienced aggressive physical contact with a student. Chronic absenteeism, verbal outbursts, the destruction of teacher or school property, and aggressive threats made by students all weighed in as predominant negative student behavior issues. Between 50% and 83% of those surveyed noted those issues as the most experienced concerns. Although less frequently reported, more than 32% of respondents said they had experienced aggressive physical contact with a student, evacuations because of unsafe behavior or serious concerns about being physically injured by a student. Erik Edoff, the MEA’s senior executive director, told reporters during a virtual press call that every student deserves a safe place to learn and that rang true of teachers and educators who spend a great deal of time each day with students. Michigan needs more behavioral health professionals. “Michigan educators are increasingly concerned about disruptive and sometimes dangerous behaviors among some of our students, these behaviors threaten both those students’ success and the success of their classmates, as well,” Edoff said. “They’re also forcing too many great educators out of a profession they love, at a time when we need to attract and retain the best and brightest to work in our neighborhood schools and keep our kids successful.” Edoff added that teachers and school support staff are seeing disruptions among students of all ages and in all kinds of school settings from school buses and classrooms to front offices and school sporting events. MEA has also said that the contributing factors to newly concerning student behavior issues included mental health challenges, constant access to smartphones and technology and overexposure to social media. Factor in cuts to recreational and recess time, along with a lack of support from communities and families, and the problem becomes more pronounced. Edoff said MEA is committed to working with its members to address the issue, but he noted that it would also take some serious conversations and work with policymakers to assist them. “It’s clear from both the surveys and the stories we’ve heard that educators need more resources from policymakers and support from administrators and families,” Edoff said. “Our public schools continue to struggle with inadequate and inequitable funding that leaves classrooms overcrowded and without enough trained quality educators to meet students’ very individualized needs. We must properly fund our neighborhood schools, so we have enough quality educators to help each and every student.” The Michigan Legislature, through the past two years of divided government and in the previous legislative trifecta years of 2023-24 — when both the state House and Senate and the governor’s office were under Democratic control — has prioritized preK-12 education and made investments in things like school lunches and expanded mental health programs. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE MEA will have a new set of leaders to help them chart a path forward on student behavior in January. The Democrats expanded their majority in the state Senate while also flipping the House after it was in Republican control over the past two years. Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson is set to hit the ground running after her inauguration early next year. Democrats have by and large made expanding education funding, and more specifically giving it an equitable funding model, during the past few budget cycles. Michigan Advance asked Edoff if the MEA had a specific appropriation request in mind, and possibly a specific percentage increase over the last few budget years that might help them in their efforts to curb poor behavior. Edoff said that although it was true that the Legislature had improved on preK-12 funding year over year, money that has helped with the situation, funding over the long road has not kept up with inflation and has not kept up with how schools were funded in the past. “A large percentage of the funding that we have received is taken up by additional categoricals that go to programs and other things that not all districts benefit from, and healthcare costs,” Edoff said. “Healthcare costs for employees of districts, both our members and other types of jobs, have gone up so dramatically and have eaten into many of the costs or many of the dollars that have flowed in in recent years.” Doug Pratt, MEA’s director of public affairs, also said that the state must remain conscious that every district is in a different financial situation in terms of what has been invested. State funding becomes strained when you look at different district staffing levels and their ability to recruit through shortages. “From a global standpoint, we don’t really break this out into a, ‘We need X million dollars to do this,’” Pratt said. “It is a district by district situation. We do need to make sure, overall, that we’re better and more equitably funding public education to catch back up to where we were even 25 years ago, when you adjust for inflation.” Deb Lotan, executive director of the Avondale/Rochester Education Association, added that intermediate school districts used to have center-based programs, and she said that those no longer exist for the most part in Michigan. Those programs — which gave structured specialized support to students outside the traditional education setting — were situated in students’ home schools, and required more support and additional funding. “I can’t say that there’s a magic number when it comes to that, but talking to colleagues, there are districts in the state of Michigan that do not have dedicated social workers, like not even a social worker for a district,” Lotan said. “So they have to rely on support from the ISD or outside entities, and that’s important because, as I said at the beginning, social workers don’t have a caseload number. And if you have a district that doesn’t have the financial means to be able to provide a social worker in their district, it costs money.”

Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
articles.description: Trump contradicted his own government's intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.
articles.content: U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy. “He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims. The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report. Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang. “A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. articles.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
articles.description: Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips.
articles.content: On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop "more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”Read full article Comments

articles.title: Another SE Michigan community has elevated lead levels in water samples
articles.description: Gibraltar is the latest Michigan city to exceed the lead-in-water limit imposed by the state. There is no safe level of lead in drinking water.
articles.content: 1009446(wavebreak3 - stock.adobe.com / 159050704)The Detroit suburb of Gibraltar is the latest Michigan city to show elevated levels of lead in drinking water sampling.There is no safe level of lead in drinking water. But taken together, the Gibraltar samples exceed the "action level" for lead. The action level is a water treatment standard that triggers public notification.Water samples taken in July show high lead levels in five homes in Gibraltar out of 20 tested in total. The city issued a public notice in October.Gibraltar is one of more than 100 communities that get water from the Great Lakes Water Authority. City officials didn’t make anyone available for comment last week.Michigan’s Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy lowered the lead action level for water systems to 12 parts per billion after the Flint water crisis. Federal regulators followed suit, and the action level is expected to drop to 10 parts per billion in 2027.Over the past year, a handful of other GLWA communities have also sampled high for lead.Lead action notices for the 12/31/2025 monitoring period:TaylorGarden CityGrosse Pointe WoodsHamtramckRiver RougeMadison HeightsInksterGrosse Ile TownshipState regulators say they'll certify and publish the latest rounds of water sampling by January.Going over the action level is a signal that water treatment isn't keeping lead from leaching from water pipes or indoor plumbing into tap water coming out of the faucet.Using an NSF-certified filter is the best way to protect yourself from lead in drinking water. Boiling water does not remove lead.

Russia fends off swarms of Ukrainian drones a day across its vast territory. But some get through
articles.description: Russia fends off swarms of Ukrainian drones a day across its vast territory. But some get through AP News Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 15, 2026 Institute for the Study of War Ukraine fires 1,336 drones into Russia in one of war's largest attacks, Moscow says ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Ukraine strikes Russian military airfield in Astrakhan Oblast, drone launch site in Oryol Obl
articles.content: Swarms of buzzing Ukrainian drones have filled the skies from the Black Sea to Moscow in recent nights in an unrelenting aerial blitz that poses a serious test of Russia’s defenses. A record high number of Ukrainian drones shot down by the military overnight Monday was topped 24 hours later, when it reported downing 1,441 of them, the most brought down since the start of the full-fledged invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Among the targets hit was a landmark bridge to Crimea that was seriously damaged in a blow to Moscow’s pride. The Russian military, in turn, ramped up its missile and drone strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, seeking to disrupt electricity and heat as winter sets in. Two key bridges in Kyiv were seriously damaged by Moscow’s attacks. The surge in aerial attacks follows a week that saw little progress in the first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months. Here’s a look at Russia’s air defenses as it fends off challenges posed by Ukraine’s attacks: Russia has more land than any other country in the world, and protecting that vast space is a major challenge despite its massive arsenal of defensive systems. “Russia’s air defense system, like many air defense systems around the world, is not necessarily designed to protect the entirety of Russia’s territory and the air approaches to the country,” said Thomas Withington, an associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute. While Ukrainian drones cruise at about 150 kph (about 95 mph), they fly very low, making it harder for radar to spot them. Their range allows them to strike deep inside Russia. In one recent attack, they hit an oil refinery in Omsk in eastern Siberia, about 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) from the border. While their payload of about 50 kilograms (110 pounds) is relatively small, their precision allows them to inflict massive damage to such facilities and other infrastructure. Ukraine also has used long-range Flamingo cruise missiles, capable of reaching up to 950 kph (590 mph), carrying a much heavier payload. Kyiv has fewer of these missiles than drones. Like in previous attacks, the number of Ukrainian drones reported downed by Russia early Monday couldn’t be independently verified, and official reports haven’t said how many actually got through air defenses to hit their targets. Withington noted that as a general rule of thumb, 10% get through and hit their targets. “It’s a game of averages,” he said, so launching more drones means that more get through. He said Russia’s air defenses, like most integrated air-defense systems around the world, are designed to shoot down aircraft, air launched weapons and ballistic missiles, and thus could struggle to engage drones. “Drones are a very different calculus, and because of it, the performance of those systems is never going to be as optimal as it would be against a conventional threat,” he said, adding that while air defenses shoot down or jam most of them, some will always get through. While Russian air defenses around key facilities such as refineries have been bolstered, Ukrainian drones have continued to set them ablaze. The large size of the targets makes them more vulnerable, Withington said, adding that Ukraine has learned a lot about the operation of Russia’s air defense systems, enabling the military to polish its tactics and find loopholes. “All of Russia’s air defenses, all of the systems they deployed, by and large have given up their secrets” after years of fighting, he said. “The more of that information and data you are armed with, the easier it becomes to defeat Russian air defenses.” In June, a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil terminal in St. Petersburg and also hit a nearby naval base, casting a cloud over President Vladimir Putin’s showcase economic forum in his hometown. Putin acknowledged the damage from the attacks, saying Russia would strengthen its air defenses. Over the past two nights, Ukraine used missiles and drones to hit the Kerch Bridge that links the mainland and the Crimean Peninsula that Moscow illegally annexed in 2014. One section of the bridge collapsed Tuesday, halting vehicular traffic. “Unfortunately, no system in the world can provide 100% protection for various facilities against such massive strikes,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. From the early stages of the conflict, Russian authorities have prioritized protecting Moscow. Media reports said additional air defense systems have been put on the outskirts of the capital, and some could be seen on top of some of the Moscow buildings, including the Defense Ministry’s headquarters facing the Gorky Park across the Moskva River. While Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin repeatedly claimed that the bulk of the drones were downed, it’s impossible to independently verify his claims. Despite the dense protection around the capital, Ukrainian drones have managed to pierce the shield. Russia scaled down the annual May 9 Victory Day parade, fearing Ukrainian drone strikes. Days later, a massive drone attack on Moscow’s suburbs killed three people. Successive attacks repeatedly struck the oil refinery on the outskirts of the capital, disrupting its operation. Another top priority has been to protect Putin’s residence in Valdai in northwestern Russia. In December 2025, Russian authorities reported a massive Ukrainian attack on the residence but claimed that none of the 91 drones hit the target. Since Soviet times, Russia has developed a broad array of air defense systems, from portable ones to long-range weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles. The S-400 Triumph is the main long-range air defense system capable of spotting and engaging aircraft and ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 400 kilometers (about 250 miles). The even more potent S-500 Prometheus system that reaches as far as 600 kilometers (about 370 miles) also is available in small numbers. Russia also uses various models of S-300 air defense missile systems, an older but still very advanced and powerful long-range weapon. For shorter ranges, the military has relied on the Pantsyr, the Tor and the Buk air defense systems. While Buk and Tor use missiles to shoot down aerial targets, Pantsyr can use a combination of guns and missiles. A Pantsyr system sits atop the Defense Ministry building in Moscow. Russia also has deployed teams armed with shoulder-fired Igla and Verba air defense missiles and machine guns for protection of key facilities. Helicopter gunships also are involved. Withington said Ukraine and Russia could be expected to further ramp up the number of attacking drones to overwhelm air defenses. “The long-term direction of travel, both for Ukraine and Russia, will be a continued exponential increase in the number of drones that can be launched at any given time,” he said.

articles.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
articles.description: OpenAI will embed six Apollo Research evaluators to investigate whether its AI models engage in subversive behavior, but restrictions on access and disclosure raise questions about their independence.
articles.content: OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing. OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI. The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic, which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat. The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user. Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions. Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers. With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI. Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release. At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits. Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations. Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work. Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged. In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.” In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.” The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable. Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route follow-up through OpenAI. That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside independent AI safety research group Redwood. Buck Shlegeris, CEO of Redwood, said in a post on Monday that the agreements announced don’t meet the bar of granting third parties “employee-like access,” saying it’s “disappointing but not surprising.” OpenAI said that they'd have embedded evaluations with employee-like access; the agreements announced today obviously don't meet that bar.This is disappointing but not surprising.Maybe future agreements will be better. https://t.co/kmDbg1Dqav The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.” That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators. While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working toward running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future. This article has been updated to include pilots with METR, Goodfire, and Transluce, as well as with information from OpenAI and comment from Redwood. articles.title: The Mids: How the Michigan election results certification process works
articles.description: In the last edition of The Mids, Michigan Public's Dustin Dwyer discusses whether there were any hiccups with the election and why count numbers may change.
articles.content: (Kalloli Bhatt / Canva)Welcome to the final edition of The Mids.As I’ve been reflecting on the election, I’ve thought about the previous elections I’ve covered in Michigan over the past two decades.I learned early on as a reporter that no election ever comes without a few minor problems. Machines break down, ballots are miscast, people make mistakes typing numbers into their computers. If you have millions of people filling out ballots and feeding them into thousands of machines, overseen by hundreds of workers in 83 counties in Michigan, mistakes are just going to happen.That’s why the results we see the day after the election are called “unofficial.” It’s why each county has a process for certifying the reported results, and why the state has its own certification process for the results it gets from the counties. After the certification, the state also carries out an audit of a random selection of paper ballots to verify the results.But were there mistakes?Even though the election was nearly two weeks ago, that process of certifying and auditing the election is still not done. Final certification is scheduled for a week from today, on Nov. 23.So it’s a little early to say this, but the thing I’ve really been thinking about since last Tuesday is just how unbelievably smooth this election turned out to be.After all the emails we received worried about federal interference, the reality is this election looks like it might be one of the smoothest I can remember in Michigan.Last week, I emailed all 83 county clerks in Michigan to check in. Most who responded were still in the process of certifying votes. But only one county told me they even expect to have a recount - Roscommon.Recounts aren’t even that rare. But in Michigan this year, it seems they are.That doesn’t mean the election was perfect, no election ever is.When the final vote is certified next week, and audited after that, you will likely see different numbers than what were reported last Tuesday. But if that happens, it probably won’t be because of any nefarious deeds or broken machinery.Why the numbers change“It's important to understand that when there are errors in the reporting of unofficial results, it doesn't mean that the ballots were counted inaccurately,” said Michigan elections director Jonathan Brater during the statewide certification process in 2024. “The voting equipment did count these votes accurately and the numbers on the results tapes that come out of those tabulators and that are reviewed during the canvas were correct.”The errors come in, Brater said, when clerks read the tabulated results and type them into their reporting systems.“And this is being done very late at night or in the wee hours of the morning after a very long day, which itself followed long weeks and long months of continuous intense work,” Brater said. “So occasionally under these circumstances, we do see a few human errors in how these unofficial results get reported.”This is why counties do a canvas after the election, to catch any errors before certifying the result.We’ll have to wait to find out just how well-run this election was. But past elections have shown only tiny differences in the end. The 2024 election audit found vote totals off by less than a dozen votes per candidate in a sample of more than 120,000 ballots.The possibility for minor differences is one reason Michigan law calls for automatic recounts for close races. That didn’t come into play this year, but it is one more reason to feel secure about Michigan’s election process.Saying goodbye 👋Thank you so much for joining us on the journey of The Mids this election season.At the start of this project way back in June, I said The Mids would be about answering the questions you’re too afraid to ask your smart political friends.But after reading the questions you sent in, I think you are the smart political friends.It turned out some of the questions you struggled with are the same questions that challenged me and my fellow reporters:How do you find out who's really funding a campaign?How do you research non-partisan judges?How would this election be protected from interference?While we weren’t able to get to all the questions you submitted, I deeply enjoyed researching the ones we did. We certainly couldn’t have done The Mids without your participation.I hope you’ll continue to follow our political coverage here at Michigan Public. If you’re not already subscribed to It’s Just Politics, our weekly newsletter that dives into Michigan’s politics, I think you’ll like it. We’ll add you to the list, but you can always opt-out.And if we start up another limited-series like The Mids, you’ll be the first to know!Have feedback and smart ideas about how we could make this newsletter better? ➡️Take our short survey, please!See you around,Dustin Dwyer, Reporter_______________________________Today’s newsletter was written by Dustin Dwyer, produced by Kalloli Bhatt, and edited by Michelle Keller.

articles.description: ChatGPT will ban an account trying to access CSAM content for 24 hours as a warning.
articles.content: OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement. The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM. OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images. What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently. OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages. The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI. OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children. The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint, updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content, retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content, and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens. articles.title: Will Lawrence outlines first priorities for Michigan's 7th district
articles.description: Lansing activist Will Lawrence flipped the 7th Congressional District of the U.S House defeating Republican Congressman Tom Barrett. He plans to focus on data centers, solar and healthcare costs in his first 100 days.
articles.content: Michigan Democratic House candidate William Lawrence greets supporters at an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Lansing, Mich.(Kristen Norman / AP)Michigan's 7th Congressional District in the U.S. House is back in the hands of a Democrat after progressive activist William Lawrence beat Republican incumbent Tom Barrett. The district encompasses seven different counties, including all of Clinton, Ingham, Livingston and Shiawassee counties, as well as parts of Eaton, Genesee and Oakland counties. Stateside Host April Baer spoke with Lawrence about whether he plans to support U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) for Speaker of the House. Jeffries is currently the House Minority Leader. Since the election, many Democratic voters have voiced criticism against Jeffries, but so far no other official is challenging him. "He is the only one who has put his name in the hat to be the speaker, and I have heard calls from constituents hoping that there will be an alternative, but I just haven't heard it," he said. "I do believe that the American people voted for change and they want confidence that we are actually going to pursue an aggressive agenda to get money out of politics, lower costs, clean up the corruption, and end the wars."Campaigning on affordability, Lawrence defeated Barrett in one of the highest spending district races in the entire United States without taking any corporate money. "It required an unprecedented grassroots movement," Lawrence said. "We knocked on 350,000 doors, and a lot of people dug deep to make their own individual contributions — it shouldn't have to be that hard." According to data from the Federal Election Commission, Barrett's individual campaign spent more than $7.2 million, double the amount spent by the Lawrence campaign. Looking ahead to his first 100 days in office, Lawrence said he's planning to make it easier for people to have more access to renewable energy resources. "With the global oil markets being so volatile as they are right now it's just a no brainer to be able to make it easier to access cheapest form of electricity that exists, which is solar energy," he said. "That program was working well — it was undone for no reason by The President." In 2025, the Trump administration rescinded a $7 billion Biden-era grant program that was intended to make it easier for low-income people to access solar power energy infrastructure and savings. In September 2026, federal courts struck down the Trump's administration cancellation of the program ordering the administration to release the grant funding. Lawrence plans on pushing for legislation that would impose a federal moratorium on new data centers, an issue he said he's expecting to see significant pushback from other legislators. William Lawrence, Democratic candidate for U.S. House of Representatives in Michigan's 7th District speaks on the campus of Michigan State University during a campaign event Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, in East Lansing, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)(Paul Sancya/AP Photo/Paul Sancya / AP)"So that we can put appropriate regulations in place to ensure that people and our environment will not be sacrificed for the benefit of billionaires in Silicon Valley and Wall Street," he said. "These tech companies are some of the biggest contributors of money in politics, and too many of my colleagues here in D.C. are taking their money." Lawrence is also hoping to support efforts that would restore healthcare subsidies offered through the Obama-era Affordable Care Act that were undone by the Trump administration to make it easier for people to pay for healthcare. "I remember a mechanic I spoke with on the campaign trail here in Lansing who was paying $800 a month for health care," he said. "And then after that vote was taken by Republicans in the House and Senate and signed by the president, his monthly premiums went up to $2,500 — he's not insured anymore because he just can't pay that." Full interview with William LawrenceApril Baer: Michigan's seventh Congressional District of the U.S. House is back in the hands of a Democrat. Progressive activist William Lawrence beat Republican incumbent Tom Barrett 51% to 47%. Will Lawrence, good to have you.Will Lawrence: Thank you for having me back.Baer: People who live in the 7th may be aware that this is a large district, with constituencies in seven different counties, which is kind of unusual under our latest version of redistricting. Your support in Ingham and Eaton counties was strong, but there were many other parts of the district who voted for your opponent. What message do you have for people who may not have voted for you about the things that you're going to do and the concerns that will be top of mind when you get to Washington?Lawrence: I'm here to represent everybody in the district. That's the job. We've had too many instances of representatives and presidents who believe their job is only to represent those who voted for them, rather than all of the people. So I've said it repeatedly on the campaign, and I'm now focused on making my first priority to set up an excellent in-district office, so that when I'm sworn in in January, we'll be ready to get started immediately with fielding people's needs. That can involve navigating Social Security, navigating Medicare and Medicaid, helping small businesses figure out how to cut red tape to get started, and generally helping people make government work for them and connect to the resources that they have worked for and earned. I'm going to do that regardless of who you voted for. And I look forward to getting right down to it here in D.C. I'm going to be fighting on issues that I've heard broad support on across the partisan spectrum. That includes getting this big money out of politics, because we could all agree by the end of the election that these ads and these mailers are just sickening. Frankly, there's too much. There are too many lies. And it doesn't make us any smarter. In fact, it pits us against each other while making us dumber. We have got to get money out of politics to put public service first, rather than who can be the best fundraiser and has the most rich friends. Unfortunately, too often that's who wins in our elections.Baer: I did just want to note that this district that you have just won was one of the highest-spending races in the entire U.S.: $61 million in political advertising. Now, I understand that a lot of that was not you. It was outside groups spending on the race. But what do you think you can do about the amount of money it takes to get elected and stay in office?Lawrence: We've got to ban super PACs. We've got to ban corporate PACs from spending in our elections. We need to have equal, equitable public funding for our elections, so everybody has the same amount of money to spend. So it's the best organizer and public servant and coalition builder who wins, rather than the person who's able to raise the most money. And we've got to overturn Citizens United, if necessary, in order to allow the rest of this to be accomplished. It's going to be a big fight, because obviously the richest people in the world are the ones who are buying our elections, and they want to keep doing it. But we can all agree that this is a disgraceful way to run a democracy, and we have got to get the money out of politics. Until we do, the people will never be able to have their say in full. Again, I'm very proud I was able to win this election in spite of not taking any corporate money. But it required an unprecedented grassroots movement. We knocked on 350,000 doors, and a lot of people dug deep to make their own individual contributions. It shouldn't have to be that hard. It should be about a debate, about ideas and about service rather than a scramble to raise. The most money should be what determines our elections.Baer: Will, you have a long record of advocacy on climate issues. A lot of people have talked about the possibilities for the new Congress, and restoring the clean energy tax credit is certainly something that you have discussed as well. I want to know if you think that that's a realistic goal for the new Congress in the first 100 days, or maybe in the first year.Lawrence: I believe so, because this was something that was benefiting businesses and consumers of energy, and it was undone in a really reckless way by President Trump. We all can agree that making it easier for people to have renewable energy is a good goal, because the best thing about solar is that it doesn't need to pass through the Strait of Hormuz before it arrives where it needs to go. So with global oil markets being as volatile as they are right now, it's just a no-brainer to make it easier to access the cheapest form of electricity that exists, which is solar energy. That program was working well. It was undone for no reason by the president, and again, because of his massive donations from the fossil fuel industry, who wanted to aggressively attack clean energy. We also heard that people are really suffering as a result of costs resulting from this war in Iran. articles.description: The point-to-point driver assist is coming to the US and Germany in 2027.
articles.content: Mercedes-Benz provided flights from Washington, DC, to San Francisco and accommodation so Ars could try its new driver assistance systems. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel. While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak. “Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Commentary: Michigan’s new lawmakers must deliver on affordability
articles.description: Last week, at least 4.8 million Michiganders cast their ballots, and preliminary reports certainly indicate a record-breaking turnout. In January, a new governor will take office and a new Legislature will be sworn in, including many lawmakers who will step into their roles for the first time. But whatever your opinion of the results, things […]
articles.content: Michigan Capitol building. (Photo by Susan J. DemasLast week, at least 4.8 million Michiganders cast their ballots, and preliminary reports certainly indicate a record-breaking turnout. In January, a new governor will take office and a new Legislature will be sworn in, including many lawmakers who will step into their roles for the first time. But whatever your opinion of the results, things did not magically change on election day. It’s no secret that “affordability” was a key theme during campaign season, but for Michiganders, the affordability crisis has been brewing for some time. All around the state, from Detroit to Ironwood, people continue to face stagnant wages and higher costs for basics like food, housing, and childcare. Our new administration and lawmakers must take note that affordability is more than a line on campaign mailers. Michiganders need them to make economic security a top priority. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The median wage in Michigan has increased by just 3.87% since 1978 when adjusted for inflation. According to the 2026 United for ALICE report, 1.63 million Michigan households — 40% of the state — are either in poverty or struggling to make ends meet. Most of them are working, but not able to get ahead. A recent report from the Michigan League for Public Policy explored the affordability crisis and identified important solutions. We hope our new leaders will take note. Let’s address work. A full-time job should cover rent, food, and utilities, but for many workers in Michigan, it doesn’t. A living wage is vital if we want to keep families and communities strong. Beyond wages, Michiganders need to know that their job is safe if they need time to recover from a serious illness, to welcome a new child, or to take care of a loved one. A statewide paid family and medical leave program will strengthen economic security, support the workforce, and improve health for parents, children and caregivers. Costs are clearly a significant barrier for many, and not just due to recent spikes caused by tariffs and inflation. Childcare, for example, has been out of reach for many families for decades. Right now, for a full-time worker earning minimum wage, infant care in a center eats up over 49% of their household budget. That’s $14,000 per year to care for just one child. And at the same time, childcare workers are woefully underpaid and receive few benefits. The state can dedicate revenue for childcare and invest directly in the early childhood workforce. Crowd gathered in Lansing for the Michigan United Coalition’s annual Capitol Day and Mothering Justice Action Fund’s annual Mamas March. April 29, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance Childcare isn’t the only cost creating roadblocks for families. Housing costs are skyrocketing, with the median Michigan rent increasing 31.5% since 2019. It’s time to slow the pace of housing costs, improve the supply of housing and make sure tenants have the protections they need to stay in their homes. But housing expenses don’t end at the monthly payment. Utility bills also continue to rise, driven by aging infrastructure and increased equipment prices. The state can make sure providers are able to maintain services without passing the burden on to households. Along with enacting new solutions, lawmakers also have a responsibility to protect the programs that already work. Medicaid and SNAP keep millions of Michiganders healthy and fed, but our new leaders need to push back on the federal cuts and red tape that are putting both programs at risk and work to mitigate the harm from these changes. Rx Kids, which gives cash to new moms and babies, has shown excellent results in health and economic security and should be expanded statewide. And we know that the federal Child Tax Credit (CTC) has a history of reversing poverty — it’s time to create a state-level CTC to help families make ends meet. We know this work is hard, and we know Michigan will have to pay for it. That starts with looking at our tax system, which needs to be modernized to generate more revenue. In the short term, that can mean raising taxes on unhealthy habits and industries like tobacco and vape products, as well as gambling. Longer term, it could mean a true overhaul of the current flat tax, which benefits wealthy corporations and individuals while leaving workers with low incomes to pay an unfair share. The election on November 3 answered the question of who will have a seat in the Capitol, but we hope that January will allow us to see true leadership. Lawmakers will not agree on every detail, nor should they. But they must agree that solving Michigan’s affordability crisis should be their number one job. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

Eritrea eliminates trachoma: a major public health milestone
articles.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has validated Eritrea's elimination of trachoma as a public health problem, making it the 11th country in WHO’s African Region and the 34th globally to reach this major milestone. “I congratulate the Government and people of Eritrea on this historic achievement,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “After two decades of determined effort, Eritrea has consigned trachoma as a public health problem to history. This is a victory for the communities most affected by this devastating disease, and a powerful example of what sustained national commitment can achieve.” In Eritrea, many people live in remote rural areas where access to health care and clean water and sanitation can be limited, creating conditions that facilitate the transmission of trachoma. Following baseline surveys conducted in different parts of the country between 2006 and 2020, Eritrea progressively implemented WHO’s recommended SAFE strategy in communities where interventions were needed. The strategy comprises surgery for trachomatous trichiasis, antibiotics to clear infection, facial cleanliness to reduce transmission, and environmental improvement, particularly improved access to water and sanitation. “I congratulate Eritrea on this historic public health milestone. It shows what is possible through sustained political commitment, community leadership and strong partnerships,” said Dr Mohamed Janabi. “Eritrea’s achievement brings us closer to a world free from the suffering caused by neglected tropical diseases and sends a strong message of hope to other African countries working towards trachoma elimination. With determination and collective action, we can protect the health and well-being of communities and leave no one behind.” Eritrea’s programme adopted a community-led sanitation approach that helped achieve significant public health gains with limited external funding. Health workers used digital tools for data collection and mapping to identify affected communities and target resources, including in hard-to-reach areas. The country surveyed all 58 sub-zobas (second-level administrative areas) and scaled up interventions wherever trachoma was endemic. The antibiotics distributed were predominantly oral azithromycin, donated by Pfizer Inc. through the International Trachoma Initiative. Eritrea has also established systems to identify and manage new trichiasis cases and will continue surveillance following validation. "This success belongs first and foremost to the people of Eritrea. The elimination of trachoma as a public health problem is the result of strong national leadership and ownership, and collaboration between communities, the Ministry of Health, the Fred Hollow's Foundation, development partners and health workers across the country,” said Dr Mary Stephen, WHO Representative to Eritrea. “WHO is proud to have supported Eritrea throughout this journey and will continue to work closely with the Government and partners to sustain these gains.” Trachoma is the world’s leading infectious cause of blindness. It is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis and spreads through contact with eye and nasal discharge from infected individuals. Repeated infections can lead to scarring of the inner eyelid, causing the eyelashes to turn inward (trichiasis), which can ultimately result in blindness. The disease is closely associated with poverty and inequities in access to basic services, including water, sanitation and hygiene and health care, and it remains endemic in some of the world's most vulnerable communities. WHO validates elimination only after receiving a recommendation from an independent, WHO-appointed dossier review group on the evidence submitted by a country, confirming that the agreed epidemiological thresholds have been met and that systems are in place to detect and manage future cases. Validation provides independent confirmation that a country has achieved the criteria for eliminating trachoma as a public health problem. Based on the latest WHO data, the global population requiring interventions against trachoma fell from an estimated 1.5 billion in 2002 to below 100 million by November 2025, a reduction of about 94%. However, as of March 2026, 92 million people still lived in trachoma-endemic areas and were at risk of trachoma blindness, and trachoma remained a public health problem in at least part of 29 countries. In 2025, 98 829 people received surgery for the advanced stage of the disease and 47.4 million received antibiotics. Trachoma is one of the 21 diseases and disease groups currently covered by the road map for neglected tropical diseases 2021–2030. NTDs affect more than 1 billion people, particularly people living in poverty and in remote or fragile settings with limited access to essential health services. The road map for neglected tropical diseases 2021–2030, endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2020, sets global targets for the prevention, control, elimination and eradication of these diseases. articles.title: What is an LLM? A practical guide to language models
articles.description: Learn what a large language model (LLM) is, how LLMs work, how they are trained, the main architectures, real examples, and their limitations.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. A large language model (LLM) is an artificial intelligence system trained on a vast dataset to analyze, predict, and generate natural language. Popular LLMs include OpenAI’s GPT models, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini, which are often used for things like writing, editing, and coding. Initially, LLM datasets mainly included text from sources like books, blogs, and even online forums. Modern LLMs now use multimodal data to expand use cases, such as powering conversational voice agents or making music. Before implementing this technology, organizations often need answers to questions like: what is an LLM, how does an LLM work, and what architectures should the team use? This guide tackles these questions while also showing real-world applications of the technology and their tangible benefits. A large language model is an AI program built on deep learning neural networks for analyzing, predicting, and generating natural language. Developers trained these models on datasets that contain billions of works across books, academic papers, websites, and blogs. The term “large” refers to both the massive volume of data used to train these models and the billions of internal parameters that govern their behavior. Large language models are a major shift from how earlier software worked; traditional software relied on explicit syntax commands but LLMs do not. Rather than processing each word in isolation, LLMs use contextual relationships to recognize complex linguistic patterns and grammar. They interpret unstructured human language and continue to respond to open-ended user prompts, adapting to context changes mid-conversation. These advancements in natural language processing power ElevenAgents so that they understand complex customer intents and execute automated workflows. Large language models process text through artificial neural networks to analyze natural language input and generate relevant content. The process begins with tokenization, where the model splits input text into smaller units called tokens. The model then translates these tokens into numerical representations (called embeddings) to evaluate mathematical or statistical relationships across tokens. Most modern LLM systems rely on the transformer neural network architecture. Transformers use self-attention mechanisms, which handle the work of evaluating the contextual relationships between tokens. The model predicts the most statistically probable token to complete a sequence by using learned patterns to calculate probability distributions. Self-attention makes it possible for natural language processing models to maintain long-range context and adapt to shifts in the middle of a conversation. Platform integrations with ElevenAgents build on these capabilities to deliver low-latency, relevant responses that mirror natural human conversation. LLM temperature is a variable setting that developers can configure to determine how random an LLM’s outputs will be. LLMs generate the next token in a string of words by selecting the option that is most common. However, for every choice the LLM makes, there could be several other alternatives that have similar weighting. By adjusting the LLM temperature, you change how strongly an LLM favors the most probable option. A low temperature setting would produce a standard and consistent output (as it would lean toward always choosing the most predictable next token in a string). On the other hand, a high temperature would deviate from the expected choice more frequently, producing more creative and varied outputs. You should adapt your LLM temperature value to the task you want to achieve. Anything that needs an element of creativity should lean toward higher temperatures, while routine tasks or structured outputs (like data summaries) should lean lower. Training LLMs requires a multistage process to transform raw text and multimodal data into functional language systems. Companies need advanced supercomputing capacity running for several months, whereas fine-tuning is a lighter process that customizes the existing base model. Frontier AI companies tend to treat their exact training process as proprietary information and most do not disclose source code or weights. Nevertheless, training generally follows this process: Transformer architectures organize neural network layers in different ways to process inputs and produce content. Classic transformers fall into three main categories: encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder (hybrid) models. However, modern systems also incorporate efficiency architectures to scale performance. Encoder-only architectures process entire sequences at once using bi-directional self-attention. This allows the machine to weigh the relationship of each token against other past and future tokens. In practice, this optimizes models for tasks like: Tasks like these also appear in speech workflows. ElevenLabs’ Scribe speech to text model transcribes speech in over 90 languages, and its entity detection feature flags sensitive details and offensive language in transcripts. Decoder-only architectures use causal attention to process tokens, predicting each word based on past tokens. These models generate fluid conversations and serve as the main architecture behind modern conversational chatbots, open-ended writing assistants, and code generation tools. In ElevenAgents, the LLM you choose, which is typically a decoder-only model, generates the agent’s responses, while a proprietary turn-taking model handles conversation timing. Encoder-decoder models use an encoder to process input and a decoder to generate output. This dual-structure approach makes hybrid models better suited for tasks that require strict context preservation, such as document summarization, language translation, and data reformatting. Translation is a classic encoder-decoder task, and ElevenLabs Dubbing supports 90+ languages. Instead of firing every neural network parameter for each word, Mixture of Experts (MoE) routes individual tokens to smaller teams of specialized “expert” sub-networks. This delivers a reasoning depth comparable to massive models but with faster speeds and lower compute costs. Meanwhile, state-space models (like Mamba) efficiently process extremely long texts. ElevenAgents includes open-source LLMs that ElevenLabs hosts in our own infrastructure. Organizations have found a wide range of use cases for large language models. These use cases show how AI transitioned from experimental research into a standard feature across the web, software applications, and everyday devices. While AI scientists continue to study and optimize the underlying architecture, real-world LLM examples show how teams have implemented them so far: As the backbone of most AI products that consumers interact with, LLMs are a powerful piece of architecture that help in numerous workflows and use cases. But if you’re looking to build with LLMs or train your own model, you should be aware of their main limitations: There are several strategies you can consider or implementations you can make to reduce the impact of these limitations. For example, enabling RAG in an LLM and attaching an ever-expanding knowledge base would overcome the static knowledge problem. Choosing a large language model for your use case is a critical decision that you may need to adjust as your business needs and even regulatory requirements change. Avoiding vendor lock-in maintains business agility and flexibility when building conversational voice AI solutions. ElevenAgents lets you choose from supported LLMs from providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, or connect your own custom model through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This makes it easy for you to choose the optimal balance of speed, reasoning capability, and cost for your specific needs. Explore ElevenAgents to see how hosted LLMs streamline voice workflows or contact sales to start building your low-latency voice agents today. An LLM is a computer program that understands and creates human text. It works by studying huge amounts of text to learn how words fit together. When given a prompt, the LLM predicts the most likely words to follow. This enables it to produce responses that answer questions, summarize reports, draft emails, and engage in conversation. LLMs also analyze and generate other types of content, such as images and videos. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad field of computer science focused on building systems that mimic human intelligence. Meanwhile, a large language model (LLM) is a specific type of AI system focused exclusively on processing and generating natural language. In other words, for LLM vs AI: all LLMs are AI systems, but not all AI systems are LLMs. A large language model is the general category for any neural network designed for natural language processing. However, Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) is a specific family of LLMs developed by OpenAI in 2018. OpenAI has also popularized the “GPT” term by naming its model ChatGPT. A quick breakdown of GPT vs LLM is that while all GPT models are LLMs, not all LLMs are GPTs. Other LLM families include the proprietary Claude from Anthropic and the open-weight Llama from Meta and Qwen from Alibaba. ChatGPT is a generative AI application built on top of an LLM. Generative AI is the broader category for tools that generate content, such as articles, images, video, and sound. In other words, ChatGPT is both because it’s a product that uses an LLM to deliver generative AI capabilities. Fine-tuning a model modifies an LLM’s internal weights by doing additional training on a specialized dataset, which adjusts its task capabilities, tone, and overall behavior. In contrast, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects the model to an external database so that it can get relevant, accurate, and timely information to respond to user queries without changing the weights. No, standard LLMs can’t update their underlying parameters in real time or during an active conversation. An LLM’s core knowledge is static and based on its initial training. However, models adapt during chat sessions by: Tokens are the basic units of data that an LLM converts into numbers it can process mathematically. Examples of tokens include text characters, image patches, or audio frames. Because an LLM converts everything it analyzes into tokens, total volume directly dictates performance, memory usage, and cost. High token counts from long documents or media fill up the context window faster, which slows down processing and adds to compute requirements. In contrast, efficient tokenization lowers operational costs and lowers latency. Jack Limebear is on the Growth team, acting as a content writer and strategist across the blog and insights pages.
