articles.title: Kotoba is joining ElevenLabs
articles.description: ElevenLabs is acquiring Kotoba, the leading Japanese voice AI lab, to bring natural, culturally fluent AI agents and voice interfaces to Japan.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. We’re excited to announce that ElevenLabs is acquiring Kotoba, the leading Japanese voice AI lab. Together, we’ll accelerate the adoption of AI agents and voice interfaces in the world’s fourth-largest economy. The way we speak and interact with each other is deeply local. We talk in different languages, dialects, and accents, and our behavior is governed by a complex, often unstated, mix of local social and cultural norms. There are few places where local nuance is more important than in Japan. Sentences don’t always contain a subject and an object, and vocabulary changes depending on who you’re speaking to. Apologies are common because they carry little liability, and pauses signal thought rather than awkwardness. Praise is typically deflected, and saying “no” directly is often avoided. Japanese even has a phrase, kūki o yomu, or “reading the air,” which means people are expected to pick up what isn’t said. Our goal is to solve how people interact with AI in every language and culture. That means building AI that feels natural and intuitive across different cultures and contexts, so everyone can access and benefit from it. With deep voice research and knowledge of the Japanese market, the Kotoba team is a natural partner in this mission. The company was founded by AI researchers Noriyuki Kojima and Jungo Kasai in 2023, with the aim of developing voice AI for a multilingual world. As they put it, “Speech shouldn't stop where language does.” “To bring the value of AI to every person, it needs to be natural and intuitive to interact with,” said Mati Staniszewski, co-founder and CEO of ElevenLabs. “The language people speak and the social norms they follow need to be reflected in the technology’s architecture from the very start. Kotoba has done exactly that for Japan, building state-of-the-art voice models that have already been adopted by some of the world’s leading enterprises. Together, we can take that even further together and build the full interaction layer for AI in Japan.” “When we founded Kotoba, our goal was to build a frontier AI lab from Japan,” said Noriyuki Kojima, co-founder and CEO of Kotoba Technologies, Inc. “Along the way, we’ve seen the enormous potential of voice AI, and three years later, we’re more determined than ever to build technology that benefits society. I’m incredibly excited for Kotoba to join ElevenLabs. Together, we can accelerate the development and adoption of voice AI, bringing tangible benefits to people and businesses in Japan and beyond.” Kojima, who goes by Nori, holds a PhD in computer science from Cornell. He worked as a research scientist at Hugging Face, and co-built Japan’s Fugaku-LLM, an open-source model trained from scratch on the RIKEN Fugaku supercomputer. Kasai holds a PhD in computer science and engineering from the University of Washington, and was an assistant professor at Toyota Technological Institute at the University of Chicago. He is one of Japan’s most-cited researchers. “Kotoba’s team has done exceptional research on the Japanese language,” said Piotr Dąbkowski, co-founder and CTO of ElevenLabs. “It is an incredibly intricate language that poses a whole range of technical challenges when building voice models. Bringing their research together with ours will improve Japanese across the entire stack ElevenLabs builds.” “I’m incredibly excited for Kotoba and ElevenLabs to join forces and lead the next wave of voice AI in Japan and East Asia,” said Jungo Kasai, co-founder and CTO of Kotoba Technologies, Inc. “Since I began my AI research career, I’ve dreamed of building a frontier AI research lab in Tokyo and creating products that transform people’s lives, from voice AI agents to simultaneous translation. Our journey is just beginning.” Kotoba’s voice model, Koto, excels in Japanese text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and speech-to-speech for simultaneous interpretation. Several major global enterprises already use Koto, including Salesforce, where it powers Japanese-language conversations in Agentforce Voice. With Kotoba joining ElevenLabs, more of the world’s leading companies will be able to build agents that handle complex conversations in Japanese naturally. “Voice is emerging as a powerful new interface for AI, with potential to transform how people interact with technology,” said Nowi Kallen, a partner at Salesforce Ventures. “We’ve been proud to back both ElevenLabs and Kotoba, and together, they’re uniquely positioned to bring more natural, intuitive AI experiences to businesses and consumers worldwide.” This is just the first step in our long-term plan to make AI intuitive and trusted for everyday interactions across Japan. In the coming months, we plan to build out our local sales leaders and continue to invest in infrastructure in Japan. With Kotoba as part of ElevenLabs, we look forward to partnering even more closely with Japanese enterprises, and multinationals operating and expanding in Japan. States, cities move to ban cryptocurrency kiosks as scams mount
articles.description: States and cities across the country are cracking down on cryptocurrency kiosks as financial scams involving the ATM-like machines continue to mount, costing Americans nearly $389 million last year alone. Four states — Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont — enacted statewide bans this year, while dozens of communities have moved to prohibit the machines or […]
articles.content: A cryptocurrency kiosk, right, at a Royal Farms gas station in Wallops Island, Va., stands ready to accept cash for a variety of crypto products including Bitcoin, Dogecoin and Ethereum. The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. (Photo by Barb Barrett/Stateline)States and cities across the country are cracking down on cryptocurrency kiosks as financial scams involving the ATM-like machines continue to mount, costing Americans nearly $389 million last year alone. Four states — Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont — enacted statewide bans this year, while dozens of communities have moved to prohibit the machines or impose new restrictions on their use. A new law in Hawaii, which went into effect in October, bans consumers from depositing cash into kiosks to buy cryptocurrency. The crackdown comes as scammers increasingly direct victims to cryptocurrency kiosks, often located in gas stations, convenience stores and grocery stores, to deposit cash that is converted into digital currency and transferred to accounts controlled by criminals. The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. Complaints increased 23% from the previous year, while financial losses jumped 58%, according to the agency’s cybercrime report, which was released in April. Older Americans have been particularly hard hit. More than half of the complaints involved people older than 50, who reported more than $302 million in losses last year. The mounting losses have prompted policymakers across the country to pursue tighter restrictions and outright bans on cryptocurrency kiosks — efforts that consumer advocates say are urgently needed to prevent further financial harm. “Every day that these laws aren’t passed are days where victims are having money stolen from them, and that money, because it’s through cryptocurrency and the nature of the kiosk, it’s just almost impossible to get any of that money back,” said Françoise Cleveland, AARP’s government affairs director, in an interview with Stateline. Indiana became the first state to ban cryptocurrency kiosks in March, followed by Tennessee and Vermont in July and Minnesota in August. The measures mark a shift from earlier efforts to regulate the machines through transaction limits, fraud warnings and licensing requirements. At least 35 states have enacted legislation addressing cryptocurrency kiosks since 2023, including 18 that passed laws this year, according to AARP, which has advocated for stronger consumer protections. Local governments are stepping up, too. In Massachusetts, at least 20 communities have banned cryptocurrency kiosks as of August. In late October, a crypto kiosk ban took effect in Jackson, Michigan — the first of its kind in the state. Operators must remove machines by the end of January. The fast-growing city of Star, Idaho, passed a ban in September requiring kiosks to be removed by this month. Other municipalities have opted to allow the machines but add stricter restrictions, including requiring fraud warnings, identification checks or transaction limits. Attorneys general in several places, including the District of Columbia, Iowa and Massachusetts, have sued cryptocurrency kiosk operators, alleging they exploited residents and failed to implement adequate safeguards against fraud. A three-year investigation by the Iowa attorney general’s office found that 98% of transactions at Bitcoin Depot kiosks in the state were linked to scams, compared with 94% at CoinFlip kiosks. The findings, released in February, prompted the state to sue both companies. Bitcoin Depot has since filed for bankruptcy, citing increasingly restrictive state regulations and bans. The company took its kiosks offline in May. In recent years, some kiosk operators have pushed back against outright bans and some proposed restrictions, arguing that the machines serve legitimate customers and that stronger fraud safeguards, rather than prohibitions, would better protect consumers. Earlier this year, Larry Lipka, the general counsel for CoinFlip, which operates more than 5,000 kiosks in the U.S. and other countries, testified against the statewide ban in Minnesota, arguing that regulators should strengthen enforcement instead. “It is inappropriate to ban a legal product because fraud is happening. Not our fault,” Lipka said. Some operators, including CoinFlip, have also implemented holding periods during which transactions can be reversed, offer refunds to scam victims and provide 24/7 customer support. How the scams work Unlike traditional ATMs, which allow customers to withdraw or deposit money from bank accounts, cryptocurrency kiosks allow users to purchase digital currencies such as Bitcoin with cash. Some machines also allow customers to sell cryptocurrency in exchange for cash. Scammers exploit the machines by calling victims and persuading them to withdraw money from their bank accounts and deposit it into a kiosk, often providing a QR code linked to a digital wallet controlled by the criminal. Quotation It’s just almost impossible to get any of that money back. – Françoise Cleveland, AARP’s government affairs director Once the cash is deposited, the machine converts it into cryptocurrency and transfers the funds to the designated digital account, called a “wallet.” Those transactions generally cannot be reversed, making it difficult for victims to recover their money. Kiosk operators also charge transaction fees, regardless of whether the transaction was fraudulent, typically ranging from 20% to 30%, depending on the company. The scams take several forms. Criminals may impersonate law enforcement officers, government officials, bank employees or technical support representatives, falsely claiming that victims owe money, face arrest or need to move their savings to protect them from fraud. Other scammers establish romantic relationships online or promote fraudulent investment opportunities before directing victims to deposit money into the machines. In many cases, scammers remain on the phone with victims throughout the transaction, providing step-by-step instructions on where to find a kiosk and how to send the money. Beyond financial scams Although older Americans account for a disproportionate share of reported losses involving cryptocurrency kiosks, some investigators say the machines can also play a role in crimes affecting younger people. Matt Hogan, a detective with the Connecticut State Police who investigates financial crimes, said kiosks have been used in connection with financially motivated sextortion, in which perpetrators threaten to distribute intimate images or videos unless victims pay them money. The schemes can target teenagers and young adults, who may be coerced into sending money to prevent explicit images from being shared with family members, friends or classmates. The FBI has warned that financially motivated sextortion increasingly targets teenage boys, particularly those between 14 and 17. Criminals may demand payment through mobile payment applications, gift cards or cryptocurrency. “That’s definitely an up and coming problem,” Hogan said. Hogan also pointed to the use of cryptocurrency kiosks in other criminal activity, including money laundering, narcotics-related offenses and payments involving child sexual abuse material. Federal authorities have raised similar concerns. In an August 2025 notice, the federal Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network warned that cryptocurrency kiosks were being used to facilitate scams and launder suspected drug proceeds. A 2022 report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office also found that drug and human traffickers have used cryptocurrency kiosks to convert cash into digital currency and obscure the source of illicit payments. “Everybody is a potential target for fraud,” said Cleveland, of AARP. Regulation or outright bans? Despite those concerns, Hogan expressed reservations about banning cryptocurrency kiosks altogether. He said he supports many of the consumer protections being adopted across the country, but worries that outright bans could push criminals toward alternative methods of transferring money that may be more difficult for investigators to trace. Transactions involving Bitcoin and many other cryptocurrencies are recorded on public digital ledgers known as blockchains, allowing investigators to follow the movement of funds between digital wallets. Advances in investigative techniques have also given law enforcement more tools to trace cryptocurrency transactions, although identifying the people behind those transactions and recovering stolen funds is still sometimes difficult. “If these machines do get shut off, bad guys are ingenuitive,” Hogan said of potential kiosk bans. “They are able to pivot. They have no care for authority or morals, so they will pivot to a place that we likely will have less visibility.” Industry representatives have also pushed back against the growing wave of bans, warning of the economic consequences for businesses and the customers who rely on their services. That debate played out in Indiana earlier this year, where lawmakers initially considered legislation requiring kiosk operators to obtain licenses, verify customers’ identities and comply with transaction and fee limits. But after hearing testimony from law enforcement, scam victims and industry representatives, lawmakers abandoned the proposed regulations in favor of an outright ban. “I can think of no legitimate reasons, no substantial legitimate reasons,” to warrant the kiosks, Republican state Sen. Scott Baldwin said during a February committee hearing. CoinFlip, which had operated in Indiana for eight years, criticized the decision, saying it had worked with lawmakers in 17 other states to adopt consumer protections without prohibiting the machines. “We are shocked to learn that the state of Indiana would eliminate an entire industry based on a lack of understanding of digital assets and the services we already provide to 17,000 Hoosiers around the state,” a company spokesperson told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. While the Saginaw Township Board of Trustees set standards for the development of any prospective data center, Romulus has approved a 180-day moratorium on data center development. Summit Township and Napoleon Township in Jackson County have also taken action on data center development, WILX’s Riley Connell reports, with Napoleon Township passing a 12-month moratorium and Summit Township adopting new rules around noise, water use and setbacks. Updates Mere weeks after the Lansing Economic Area Partnership and Lighthouse Sustainability announced their plans to pursue public engagement for a potential data center in Delhi Township, the developer has decided to withdraw. According to a news release from the Lansing Economic Area Partnership, Lighthouse Sustainability will seek other opportunities across the country, bringing an end to the proposal. Following a data center proposal in Howell Township which has since been put on ice, township officials have directed their attorney to draft an ordinance which could ban local officials, staff and contractors from signing nondisclosure agreements, MLive’s Jennifer Eberbach reports. Saline Township Trustees have reaffirmed a 12-year, 50% tax break for the Oracle and OpenAI data center, and moved to establish an Industrial Development District for the project, despite concerns from residents that trustees had not followed the proper legal pathway for approving the abatement. The Detroit News’ Max Reinhart reports that both measures passed unanimously. More details have emerged around a large-scale development in Lenox Township that residents fear may be a data center, MLive’s Lucas Smolcic Larson reports. A conceptual plan submitted to township officials shows 10 buildings covering more than 2 million square feet. While a related application to rezone 1,400 acres in the community does not refer to the project as a data center, the company behind the proposal previously sent letters to local officials stating that it was developing a data center campus on the land matching the rezoning request. The township is scheduled to hold a public hearing on the rezoning request tonight. The University of Michigan is pursuing an archaeological review of its proposed computing center site in Ypsilanti Township, to evaluate the likelihood that Indigenous artifacts or remains could be unearthed at the site, Etai Smotrich-Barr reports for Michigan Public. The review follows a warning from the State Historic Preservation Office that the area surrounding the Huron River, which the project site borders, is “highly archaeologically sensitive.” Hyperscale Data, the parent company for the Dowagiac data center operated by Alliance Cloud Services, announced that is had sold off its remaining Bitcoin reserves in order to finance the development of its Michigan data center, which is transitioning from Bitcoin mining operations to artificial intelligence computing. Allen Park has extended its moratorium on data center development, The Detroit News’ Max Bryan reports. The city unanimously agreed to pause development for another six months, after approving its original six-month moratorium on June 9, News of Note As a data center developer proposes underwater data centers in Maine and Alaska, Michigan Advance spoke with environmental advocates about the guardrails in place were a developer to pursue a similar proposal in the Great Lakes. WDIV Local 4’s Brandon Carr reviews Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s plan on data centers, including a moratorium on new data center construction until the state establishes regulations for community transparency and environmental protections. RenCen redevelopment advances despite calls for more time and answers
articles.description: Among the matters up for a vote is a package of crucial tax incentives Bedrock and General Motors say they need for the project, which requires a total of $548 million in public subsidies.
articles.content: Detroit’s City Council could vote as soon as tomorrow on a package of vital tax incentives and community benefits proposed as part of a $2.2 billion makeover of the Renaissance Center and East Riverfront. The council’s Planning and Economic Development Committee voted to advance the controversial redevelopment proposal to the full body for consideration amid community concern over the speed of the process and an hourslong meeting. Here’s what happens now: WHAT IS GOING TO COUNCIL? Among the matters up for a vote is a package of crucial tax incentives Bedrock and General Motors say they need for the project, which requires a total of $548 million in public subsidies. Also on the docket is the historic $133 million Community Benefits Agreement the Neighborhood Advisory Council signed two weeks ago. Though these items could potentially be approved as soon as tomorrow, PED Committee Chair Latisha Johnson said during last week’s committee meeting that she anticipates discussion will be far from over on Tuesday. Johnson and President Pro Tem Coleman A. Young II voted to move the proposals to Tuesday’s formal session. Council Member Gabriela Santiago-Romero voted no. With one PED subcommittee meeting (which is where these items are emerging from) falling between the two formal sessions left before winter recess, these items could be approved before Nov. 25. WHAT’S THE RUSH? The pace and timing developers are pushing for has been criticized since the community benefits meetings began months ago. Community members and advocates — even those supporting the development — as well as Santiago-Romero echoed those criticisms several times on Thursday. Developers are seeking council approval before recess in order to be considered ASAP for state tax breaks by the Michigan Strategic Fund. WHAT DID I MISS? A lot. The Freep’s JC Reindl and I had a lot of the same takeaways, so check out his story. From the over six hours of discussion, presentations, and public comment took place at Thursday’s marathon session, here are the basics: NAC members, developers and administration members sat in for much of the meeting. They explained the background of how we got here, the reason developers say tax incentives are needed, the overview of the community benefits and more. Residents and advocates are mixed and fall into more than a few camps. Broadly: SUPPORTERS. Some speakers — many of whom were NAC members, developers, or represented big and small business, labor and union interests — expressed their excitement and enthusiasm for the development and the revitalization that comes with it. Many said they saw the project as a much-needed injection to the fight to keep Detroiters in Detroit, one of the few they said came with tangible economic and social benefits, like jobs and the entertainment district. CAUTIOUS OPTIMISTS. Even many of the supportive attendees who spoke up urged council members to take their time, do their due diligence, and not allow themselves to be rushed. Many cited contentious developments that formerly went through the city’s CBO process, like Stellantis and Herman Kiefer. THE PEOPLE PUSHING BACK. People have been pushing back against the development since before the CBO/NAC meetings began, and many who spoke Thursday said they still didn’t trust Detroiters were guaranteed direct and protected community benefits for all they would be giving away in public funding. Many took issue with the long-asked-for items they said were left out of the CBA, like revenue sharing and public ownership. Organizers with groups like Detroit People’s Platform, Detroit Action and others convened a press conference near the Spirit of Detroit statue outside the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center ahead of Thursday’s committee meeting. They demanded a delay of the vote and questioned the lack of transparency in the process, among other things. Opponents and advocates concerned over elements of the deal convened a press conference near the Spirit of Detroit statue outside the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center ahead of Thursday’s committee meeting. Credit: Jasmine Snow Several council members — including non-PED council members like Scott Benson and Denzel McCampbell — also pressed developers and the administration for answers on a multitude of issues. For example, Benson wanted more concrete details on job and training commitments. Johnson said she was voting it through so the whole body could weigh in on the issue. She also said she wanted to spend more time and energy delving deeper on the nonprofit Dan Gilbert pledged $1 billion to create in order to run the development, as well as earmarking where exactly the proposed abatement funds from developers would be going. Notably, Santiago-Romero echoed concerns of community members in her questions, and highlighted the “very, very rushed” process. She also criticized a recent exchange in which Bedrock’s CEO called McCampbell’s questions about the necessity of the use of public funding “indecent.” WHAT CAN I DO NOW? These items are officially in front of council members, so reaching out to them directly is always a decent start. City Council’s public comment period is always right up there, too. Find the agenda and attendance information here. Also, Council Member Mary Waters is hosting a RenCen Community Meeting tonight, according to an email. The meeting will be held in-person Nov. 16, from 5-7 p.m. at the Coleman A. Young Community Center, 2751 Robert Bradby Dr. Residents can also attend virtually, though registration is required. You can catch past council sessions here, if you miss it.

articles.description: The founder of the collapsed FTX crypto exchange, who is serving prison time for fraud, would have made a windfall from a $500 million investment in Anthropic.
articles.content: The founder of the collapsed FTX crypto exchange, who is serving prison time for fraud, would have made a windfall from a $500 million investment in Anthropic. David Yaffe-Bellany reports on the crypto industry. Sam Bankman-Fried, the convicted cryptocurrency fraudster, lives in a 30-person unit at the federal prison in Lompoc, Calif., a barbed-wire compound about a million miles away from his former life as a technology billionaire in the Bahamas. For the most part, Mr. Bankman-Fried, 34, tries not to think about all the “could-have-beens,” he said on a recent call. But one has become difficult to ignore. In late 2021, the heyday of his FTX crypto exchange, Mr. Bankman-Fried spent $500 million on a 13.5 percent stake in a little-known artificial intelligence start-up called Anthropic. This week, Anthropic is set for an initial public offering that is expected to value the company at $1.4 trillion, potentially one of the largest Wall Street debuts in history. At that valuation, Mr. Bankman-Fried’s investment, diluted over several years, would now be worth an eye-watering $35 billion — about the size of FTX’s entire business at its peak. But the shares are gone. They were tied up in bankruptcy court until 2024, when executives overseeing the scattered remains of FTX sold the Anthropic stake for $1.34 billion — a tiny fraction of its current value. For Anthropic, the fate of those shares is an odd quirk of history. For Mr. Bankman-Fried, it’s a source of extreme frustration and resentment. Even after a fraud conviction, a failed appeal and a succession of public humiliations, he is still trying to prove his innocence, arguing that FTX had sufficient resources to avoid bankruptcy. articles.title: NRDC urges incoming Benson administration to prioritize clean transportation
articles.description: As lawmakers and state officials begin the transition to new Democratic leadership in Lansing, a national environmental organization is offering four recommendations for Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s administration to address affordability and promote clean transportation. In a new policy brief, the Natural Resources Defense Council argues that clean transit belongs at the center of any governor’s […]
articles.content: Electric vehicle chargers in Mackinaw City, funded by the Michigan Department of Environment Great Lakes and Energy. | Kyle DavidsonAs lawmakers and state officials begin the transition to new Democratic leadership in Lansing, a national environmental organization is offering four recommendations for Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s administration to address affordability and promote clean transportation. In a new policy brief, the Natural Resources Defense Council argues that clean transit belongs at the center of any governor’s affordability agenda “because it lowers household costs while improving access, air quality, and economic resilience.” According to the NRDC, the average Michigan family spends $17,000 a year on car payments, fuel, maintenance and insurance, making up nearly a quarter of the state’s median $72,000 household income. Among Michigan residents, transportation ranked as the second-highest household expense, behind housing. “High gas and diesel prices have been extremely hard on Michigan families, and we need to do more to provide affordable options. Michigan is behind on this front, and it doesn’t have to be this way,” Abby Clark, the Michigan director of government affairs at NRDC, said in a statement. “Michigan’s next governor and legislature can increase reliable transit options, safe ways to walk and bike, and access to electric vehicles that cost less to run and maintain. We can be less vulnerable to volatile gas prices and put real money back in people’s pockets.” In the brief, the NRDC offers four policy solutions to lower transportation costs in Michigan. The first is to rewrite the state law governing how transportation tax revenue is distributed to prioritize investments to expand access to reliable public transit and safe walking and biking options and ensure tax dollars are spent on projects that will deliver the greatest impact for residents. Whitmer signs directive transitioning the state’s fleet to zero emission vehicles by 2040 Its second recommendation urges state leaders to accelerate the deployment of electric vehicle charging equipment, which the NRDC says will help families save money by making the switch to an electric vehicle an easier choice. According to the U.S. Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center, there are 5,765 public charging ports within the state. The NRDC also advised Benson and the Legislature to mitigate the impact of high diesel prices stemming from the war in Iran by supporting existing grant programs administered by the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy to reduce the price of electric trucks and help transition medium and heavy-duty vehicles to electric options. The council also encouraged the state to lead by example by electrifying the states’ own vehicle fleets, cutting down on fuel and maintenance costs for the state government and taxpayers. “Clean transportation is essential to Michigan’s climate future, our public health and our economy,” NRDC Michigan Policy Director for Climate and Energy Derrell Slaughter said. “We can’t build a clean future for Michigan by cleaning up power plants alone. The cars and trucks we drive every day matter just as much.”

articles.title: LVMH’s Media Division announces strategic partnership with OpenAI
articles.description: LVMH’s Media Division and OpenAI announce a partnership to support journalism with AI and make its publications more accessible through ChatGPT.
articles.content: This news was originally shared by LVMH’s Media Division and can be read here(opens in a new window). Paris, 16 November 2026—LVMH Group’s Media Division and OpenAI announce the signing of a strategic agreement to support new uses of artificial intelligence across all the division’s publications and make their journalism more accessible through ChatGPT. The agreement includes the deployment of OpenAI tools and ChatGPT Enterprise to teams across the media division, enabling them to develop AI applications tailored to their day-to-day work. Their shared ambition is to empower teams across the media division to experiment with and develop practical uses of AI that support journalism and high-quality reporting. Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that, when put to work in newsrooms, enables journalists to focus on the core of their profession: investigating, analysing and writing. Teams will be able to explore applications such as document research, document comparison and preliminary translation. The goal is to enable them to devote more time to investigative reporting, analysis and reporting in the field. In addition, in an increasingly crowded information landscape, personalisation has become a major priority. Artificial intelligence is an essential tool for developing and delivering products and services that meet the needs of customers, readers and advertisers alike, helping to attract and retain them and grow revenue across the publications. This partnership is a company-wide initiative that also enhances the presence of content from LVMH Group’s Media Division in ChatGPT, providing summaries and excerpts in response to relevant user questions, identifying their sources and including direct links to the original articles. The partnership will extend across all the division’s publications and support the evolution of roles throughout the organisation: streamlining operations, improving efficiency, and encouraging innovation and creativity to prepare today’s publications for tomorrow. The rollout will be supported by training tailored to everyone’s use cases. LVMH Group’s media division, Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien, brings together 17 media brands covering news, finance, culture, heritage, arts and music. With 1,800 employees, including nearly 700 journalists, it reaches more than 27 million people in France every month. The Group’s media brands: Boursier.com(opens in a new window), Capital Finance, Challenges, Connaissance des Arts, Historia, Investir, La Lettre de l’Expansion, L’Agefi, Le Parisien, Aujourd’hui en France, Les Echos, L’Opinion, medici.tv(opens in a new window), Mezzo, Mieux Vivre Votre Argent, Paris Match, Radio Classique. The Group’s exhibitions and publishing houses: Citadelles & Mazenod, Fine Arts Paris, In Fine, Salon du Dessin.
